The attack can be initiated remotely. The affected component should be upgraded. This CVE was requested by the vendor.

In the `setup-osc` GitHub Action of Eclipse Apoapsis, from commit 4e9eaff up to, but not including, commit 03efc4c, the ORT Server version returned by the `/api/v1/versions` endpoint is inserted into a shell script via a GitHub Actions expression without validation. An attacker who controls the responses of the configured ORT Server, for example by compromising the server, can execute arbitrary commands on the GitHub Actions runner and access the secrets available to the calling workflow.



The issue is fixed in commit 03efc4c, which only accepts version strings consisting of alphanumeric characters, `.`, `+`, and `-`.

Open Babel through 3.2.1 contains a use-after-free vulnerability in OBForceField::Setup() that leaves stored constraints bound to freed atoms when set up with an empty molecule. Attackers can supply a molecule file yielding an empty molecule so later SteepestDescent() or ConjugateGradients() calls read freed memory, causing crashes or incorrect results.

POCO C++ Libraries through 1.15.4 contain a denial of service vulnerability in InflatingStreamBuf::reset() and InflatingInputStream::reset() that fails to discard unconsumed compressed input after decompression errors. Attackers can supply one corrupt zlib, gzip or zip-deflate stream to applications reusing an InflatingInputStream, causing all later stream reads, including valid ones, to fail.

CESNET libyang through 6.4.13 contains an incomplete cleanup vulnerability in ly_out_reset() in src/out.c that tests a stale errno ESPIPE value after a successful seek. Applications reusing one output handler for different clients rewind but do not truncate the file, leaking leftover bytes of a previous client's output.

libyang through 6.4.13 contains a file descriptor leak in ly_in_new_filepath() and ly_in_filepath() in src/in.c that fails to close descriptors when file mapping fails. Attackers who can supply files parsed through lyd_parse_data_path() or lys_parse_path() can repeatedly submit empty files to exhaust descriptors, causing later file and socket operations to fail.

CESNET libyang through 6.4.13 contains a return of wrong status code vulnerability in ly_in_filepath() in src/in.c that reports success when a new file cannot be opened or mapped. Attackers who make an application switch a reused input handler to a nonexistent or empty file cause it to parse the previously loaded file's data as the requested input.

libyang through 6.4.13 contains a release of invalid pointer vulnerability in ly_in_memory() and ly_in_memory_chunk() in src/in.c that return the current read position instead of the previous start address. Attackers supplying YANG data parsed from a heap buffer can cause applications freeing the returned pointer to pass an interior address to free(), aborting the process.

Assimp 5.1.0 through 6.0.6 contains a memory leak vulnerability in AMFImporter::ParseFile that overwrites the previous XML parser pointer without releasing it. Attackers can supply repeated AMF files to applications using a long-lived Assimp::Importer to retain parsed documents and exhaust memory.

POCO C++ Libraries through 1.15.4 contain a denial of service vulnerability in InflatingStreamBuf::reset() that fails to clear stale buffered data from a previous failed stream. Attackers can supply one corrupt compressed stream to an application reusing an InflatingOutputStream, causing subsequent valid streams to fail decompression.

Boost.JSON 1.75.0 through 1.92.0 contains a denial of service vulnerability in monotonic_resource::release() because it does not reset next_size_ when returning blocks upstream. Attackers can send repeated JSON documents larger than the initial block, growing allocation sizes geometrically until every later allocation fails with bad_alloc.

Paid Memberships Pro before 3.8.8 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to read restricted post excerpts because restriction is reapplied only through the_excerpt filter. Attackers can request RSS or Atom feeds, oEmbed URLs, or pages rendering the Post Excerpt block to read opening text or manual excerpts of member-only posts.

JuggleIM im-server before 1.8.17 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows authenticated end users to invoke the internal upd_user_info operation because ImListenerImpl.PublishArrived forwards any client-supplied topic as the RPC method. Attackers holding a valid connect token can supply another user's id to UpdUserInfo to overwrite that user's nickname, portrait, extension fields and settings.

JuggleIM im-server before 1.8.17 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to invoke the internal g_del_members operation by supplying it as a client topic. Attackers holding a valid connect token can send crafted WebSocket or HTTP publish requests with arbitrary group and member ids to remove any users from any group in the application.

HortusFox through 6.4 contains an information exposure vulnerability in BackupModule::start that allows unauthenticated attackers to download workspace backups stored in the public/backup directory. Attackers can enumerate one-second-precision creation timestamps used as filenames to retrieve archives containing locations, plants, gallery, tasks, inventory and calendar data.

HortusFox (hortusfox-web) through 6.4 contains a password reset poisoning vulnerability in UserModel::restorePassword that builds reset links from the client-controlled Host header. Unauthenticated attackers can request a reset with a forged Host header to capture the victim's reset token and take over accounts including administrators.

Part-DB (Part-DB-server) before 2.20.6 contains an open redirect vulnerability in several controllers that pass user-supplied _redirect or redirect_back parameters to redirect() without validating local paths. Attackers can craft links to endpoints like /tools/batch_eda_edit using scheme-relative or protocol-relative values that bypass the nelmio_security guard, sending authenticated victims to attacker-controlled phishing sites.

FCEUX before 2.8.0 contains an integer overflow in SetBoardName() in src/unif.cpp that allows crafted UNIF ROM files to write past a heap buffer. Attackers can persuade users to open a .unf file with a 0xFFFFFFFF MAPR chunk length, wrapping the allocation to zero and corrupting heap memory to crash the emulator or execute code.

FCEUX 2.5.0 before 2.8.0 contains an integer overflow in iNESLoad() in src/ines.cpp that allows a crafted NES 2.0 ROM to write past a heap buffer. Attackers can persuade users to open a .nes file using exponent-multiplier PRG ROM size notation with mappers 53, 198, 228 or 547 to corrupt memory, crashing the emulator and possibly executing code.

OneDev before 17.2.4 contains an argument injection vulnerability in commit query handling that allows authenticated attackers to inject git options through branch or tag names. Attackers can push a branch named like --output=<path> and query it via the commits page or REST API to overwrite server-writable files, causing denial of service.

nconf through 1.0.0-beta.2 contains a prototype pollution vulnerability in the Memory store merge() function in lib/nconf/stores/memory.js that lacks __proto__ key rejection. Attackers controlling merge keys like '__proto__:isAdmin' or nested __proto__ properties can inject properties into Object.prototype, altering application logic or causing errors.

PyBioNetGen 0.8.7 contains a code injection vulnerability in ParameterBlock.add_item() and ModelBlock.add_item() that allows attackers to execute Python code by passing parameter expressions to sympy.sympify(). Attackers can supply a crafted BNG-XML model file with Python code in a Parameter expr or value attribute to execute code as the user when loaded with bionetgen.bngmodel().

asar-py before 0.1.4 contains a path traversal vulnerability in AsarArchive.extract() and extract_archive() that allows attackers to write files outside the destination directory via crafted archive headers. Attackers can supply a .asar archive with '..' path components or malicious symlink targets to write files such as usercustomize.py, leading to code execution.

A vulnerability was determined in FastStone Image Viewer up to 8.5. This vulnerability affects unknown code of the file FSViewer.exe of the component ICO Decoder. Executing a manipulation can lead to out-of-bounds write. The attack may be performed from remote. The exploit has been publicly disclosed and may be utilized. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A vulnerability was identified in philipjscott simple-thumbnail up to 1.6.5. This issue affects the function ffmpegExecute of the file index.js. The manipulation of the argument seek leads to os command injection. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A security flaw has been discovered in msaifulcsse Ticket-Travel-Management-System 28b68cea41b3a9eb8d533db992e0b5ba2db68854/15c7bc0b48c263233326bb227fef01efc54c24a7. Impacted is an unknown function of the file bus1.php. The manipulation of the argument dfrom/gto/ddate/rdate results in sql injection. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. This product takes the approach of rolling releases to provide continious delivery. Therefore, version details for affected and updated releases are not available. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A weakness has been identified in nliautaud pico-content-editor up to 02d5ad6c820c5050c542ab9505819b5e0a0ba1af. The affected element is the function getLanguageContent of the file src/EditorsHandlers/ContentTools.php of the component ContentTools Editor. This manipulation of the argument ContentToolsUrl causes server-side request forgery. The attack can be initiated remotely. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. Continious delivery with rolling releases is used by this product. Therefore, no version details of affected nor updated releases are available. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way. This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

A security vulnerability has been detected in Ghostty up to 1.3.1. The impacted element is an unknown function of the component macOS OSC 8 Hyperlink Handler. Such manipulation leads to injection. The attack can be launched remotely. Upgrading to version 1.4.0 is sufficient to resolve this issue. The name of the patch is 54fe8e188552977249a084db687e75aee6bf12e9. Upgrading the affected component is advised.

A vulnerability has been found in TAILG Feimeng up to 20261028. Affected is an unknown function of the component Wireless Remote Control System. The manipulation leads to authentication bypass by capture-replay. The attack needs to be initiated within the local network. The attack is considered to have high complexity. The exploitability is told to be difficult. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

A weakness has been identified in Spotweb up to 1.5.8. This issue affects the function redirect of the file lib/SpotTemplateHelper.php of the component Login. Executing a manipulation of the argument http_referer can lead to open redirect. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. This patch is called 0853d646d615225b35f466a960976d1492b786a9. Applying a patch is advised to resolve this issue.

A security vulnerability has been detected in TOTOLINK N350RT 9.3.5u.6468_B20250827/9.3.5u.6466_B20250825. The affected element is the function setLanguageCfg of the file /cgi-bin/cstecgi.cgi. Such manipulation of the argument lang leads to authorization bypass. The attack can be executed remotely. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used.

A vulnerability was detected in mahmoudai1 school-management-system up to ecec9faaf2fb1a3c5cd096e063f8ef326d09cdfd. The impacted element is the function userModel::checkUserInDB of the file loginServer.php of the component Login Handler. Performing a manipulation of the argument ID results in sql injection. The attack is possible to be carried out remotely. The exploit is now public and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

DeepSeek-Reasonix before 2.53.0 contains a command execution vulnerability that allows attackers to run commands without user approval because the shellsafe classifier treats git blame and git whatchanged as read-only. Attackers can plant a diff textconv driver in .gitattributes and .git/config so that git blame, triggered via prompt injection or routine use, executes attacker-chosen commands with the user's privileges, exposing stored provider API keys and session history.

llama.cpp from b7118 before b12604 contains an integer underflow vulnerability in llama_grammar_parser::parse_sequence() that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to cause denial of service by supplying GBNF repetitions with max lower than min. Attackers can send a grammar like {5,2} in the grammar field of a llama-server /completion request, wrapping n_opt to generate endless repetition rules that hang the process and exhaust memory.

Cron-parser through 5.10.0 contains an unbounded memory allocation vulnerability in CronExpressionParser.parse() that allows unauthenticated attackers to exhaust memory by supplying oversized cron fields. Attackers can submit a roughly 1.6 MB expression of repeated wildcard tokens that expand into huge arrays, exhausting the V8 heap and crashing the Node.js process.

ToolJet from 3.16.0 before 3.20.256 contains an improper signature verification vulnerability in StripeWebhookGuard that validates webhooks against a self-generated signature instead of the Stripe-Signature header. Unauthenticated attackers can post forged Stripe events to the POST /api/organization/payment/webhooks route to activate subscriptions, generate licenses, change plans or seats, and add AI credits without payment.

paramz through 0.10.0 contains an insecure deserialization vulnerability that allows attackers to execute code by supplying crafted model files to paramz.load(), which calls pickle.load() without restrictions. Attackers can embed objects whose __reduce__ method returns callables like exec or os.system in shared paramz or GPy model files to run code with the victim's privileges.

Wallos before 5.11.2 contains an infinite loop vulnerability that allows authenticated users or API key holders to exhaust server resources by storing subscriptions with a frequency of 0. Attackers can trigger renew.php or get_monthly_cost.php to loop forever on a P0D interval, pinning PHP workers and hanging the next-payment cron job for all users.

BookStack before 26.09.3 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated Editors to permanently delete recycle bin content by converting chapters to books or books to shelves. Attackers can trigger TrashCan::destroyEntity() through the conversion actions to force-delete soft-deleted children, revisions and attachments, including content deleted by other users, preventing restoration.

Leptonica 1.79.0 through 1.87.0 contains a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in l_byteaInitFromStream() that allows attackers to write past a heap buffer by supplying oversized input. Attackers can provide a file larger than 1,000,000,000 bytes, causing l_byteaCreate() to allocate a 201-byte buffer before memcpy copies the full stream size, crashing the application.

Chatwoot before 4.20.0 contains a missing authentication vulnerability in the Bandwidth SMS webhook endpoint POST /webhooks/sms/:phone_number that allows unauthenticated attackers to submit forged SMS events. Attackers who know an inbox phone number can set the 'to' field to inject inbound messages with forged sender numbers or forge delivery status updates.

Chatwoot before 4.20.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows account administrators to attach integration hooks to other accounts' inboxes by supplying a foreign inbox_id. Attackers can create a Dialogflow hook referencing a victim inbox, leaving its new conversations stuck as pending awaiting a bot, and enumerate inbox IDs to disclose inbox names.

Loginizer before 2.1.4 contains a brute-force lockout bypass vulnerability in loginizer_login_failed() that allows unauthenticated attackers to avoid failed-attempt recording via non-ASCII URL bytes. Attackers can append invalid UTF-8 or 4-byte sequences to wp-login.php or xmlrpc.php request URLs, causing the log INSERT to fail and enabling unlimited password guessing without lockout or email notification.

GNOME libxml2 2.9.10 through 2.15.4 contains a use-after-free vulnerability in xmlValidatePopElement because xmlCtxtReset frees the DTD without popping stale validation states. Attackers supplying an XML document ending inside an element to an application reusing a DTD-validating xmlTextReader can trigger heap reads, causing crashes and limited heap disclosure via error messages.

libxml2 through 2.15.4 contains a heap use-after-free vulnerability that allows attackers to crash applications by triggering xmlFreeNode on a stale reader->faketext node after xmlTextReader reuse. Attackers can supply XML containing a namespace declaration to applications that read its value and reuse the reader, causing a freed document's dictionary read and process crash.

libxml2 2.13.0 through 2.15.4 contains a denial of service vulnerability because xmlTextReaderSetup does not reset reader->state when a reader is reused. Attackers can submit one malformed XML document to an application reusing a single reader, causing every later document to be rejected until the reader is recreated.

GEOS 3.13.0 before 3.15.1 contains an uncontrolled recursion vulnerability in RectangleContains::isContainedInBoundary that recurses indefinitely on curved geometries returned by getGeometryN. Attackers can supply crafted WKT or WKB CircularString, CompoundCurve, or CurvePolygon geometries tested via PreparedGeometry::contains or GEOSPreparedContains against a prepared rectangle to crash the process with a stack overflow.

Boost.JSON 1.84.0 through 1.92.0 contains an information exposure vulnerability because parser_for reset() does not reset nested parse_into handlers, retaining state across documents. Attackers controlling an abandoned or subsequent document parsed by a reused parser_for can cause partial string data from one document to appear in another's result.

GNOME libxml2 2.9.10 through 2.15.4 contains a use-after-free vulnerability that allows attackers to trigger stale DTD validation states after xmlTextReaderCurrentDoc documents are freed. Attackers can supply an XML document ending with an error inside an element, causing xmlTextReaderClose to read freed element declarations, leading to crashes and possible invalid frees.

GNOME libxml2 through 2.15.4 contains a double free vulnerability in xmlReaderNewWalker() that frees reader->input again after xmlTextReaderClose() already released it. Applications reusing a closed xmlTextReader with xmlReaderNewWalker() can crash, and groomed heap memory can control the close callback for possible code execution.

GNOME libxml2 2.12.6 through 2.15.4 contains a NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in xmlTextReaderConstEncoding() after a reader is reset with xmlReaderNewWalker(). Because xmlCtxtReset() leaves ctxt->input NULL, querying the document encoding makes xmlGetActualEncoding() read ctxt->input->flags without a check, crashing the application and causing denial of service.

GNOME libxml2 2.14.0 through 2.15.4 contains a missing NUL termination flaw in xmlBufferAddHead() in buf.c that leaves uninitialized heap bytes as the terminator for storage-less buffers. Attackers supplying data to applications reusing an xmlBuffer can trigger over-reads via xmlBufferCat() and xmlStrlen(), disclosing adjacent heap memory or causing crashes.

FFmpeg through 9.1 contains an information disclosure vulnerability because avcodec_flush_buffers() does not release the decoder context's frame buffer pool, so recycled buffers retain prior picture data. Attackers can supply crafted damaged streams to applications reusing one decoder context across users to recover another user's decoded picture content from unwritten frame regions.

FreeRDP before 3.33.0 contains a heap out-of-bounds write in h264_context_reset() in libfreerdp/codec/h264.c, which stores new dimensions before the YUV planes are reallocated. Remote peers can trigger surface height increases so avc420_compress() writes taller frames past undersized luma and chroma planes, corrupting heap memory or crashing the process.

Xiph.Org libvorbis through 1.3.7 contains a heap out-of-bounds read vulnerability in ov_time_tell() in lib/vorbisfile.c that reads vf->vi[-1].rate after a failed seek leaves vf->pcm_offset at -1. Attackers can supply a crafted Ogg Vorbis file with a corrupted page to applications that seek and query playback time, leaking heap bytes via the returned value or crashing the process.

libvorbis through 1.3.7 contains a stack buffer overflow vulnerability in _ov_getlap() in lib/vorbisfile.c that passes a negative sample count from vorbis_synthesis_lapout() to memcpy(). Attackers can supply a short, valid Ogg Vorbis file with suitable block sizes to overwrite stack frames and crash applications performing two consecutive lapped seeks.

libical 4.0.0 before 4.0.7 contains an infinite loop vulnerability in icalrecur_iterator_set_range() that allows attackers to cause denial of service by supplying crafted recurrence rules. Attackers can provide a calendar whose recurrence rule is iterated over a reverse range, causing the loop to never terminate and spin the calling thread at full CPU indefinitely.

Xiph.Org libFLAC 1.5.0 contains a memory leak in FLAC__stream_encoder_finish() because free_() never releases the main thread task's frame bit writer buffer. Attackers submitting many audio streams to a long-running service that reuses one encoder can leak at least 32 KiB per stream, causing memory exhaustion.

GNOME libxml2 through 2.15.4 contains a NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in xmlParseStartTag2() that allows attackers to crash applications by triggering parser context reuse after SAX1 parsing. Attackers can supply documents with attributes parsed first with XML_PARSE_SAX1 and then without it on a reused context, causing writes to unallocated ctxt->attallocs and denial of service.

OpenCV 3.0.0 through 4.14.0 and 5.0.0 through 5.1.0 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the built-in MJPEG encoder when writing grayscale frames due to incorrect level shifting in convertToYUV(). Attackers controlling pixel content written as grayscale MJPEG video can trigger unchecked cat_table and huff_dc_tab lookups, leaking adjacent or uninitialized memory into the output file or crashing the process.

NodeBB 4.12.0 before 4.16.4 contains an execution after redirect vulnerability in the Intents.create controller that allows unauthenticated attackers to trigger ActivityPub note ingestion. Attackers can send GET requests to /intents/create with a remote note URI in the toPid parameter to inject federated content as local topics and posts.

ProjeQtOr before 13.1.2 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in tool/getAFieldForAClassById.php that allows authenticated low-privilege users to read any object property. Attackers can request Class=User with an administrator id and field=password or email to retrieve password hashes for offline cracking.

Teracom TCW122B-CM firmware before 4.07 contains a predictable session cookie vulnerability that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to hijack administrator sessions by guessing tick-counter-derived cookies. Attackers can predict or brute-force the 32-bit cookie from device uptime and login timing to control relays, settings, and administrator credentials.

'@irrelon/path 6.2.2 before 7.0.3 contains a prototype pollution vulnerability in merge() and mergeImmutable() that allows remote attackers to modify Object.prototype by supplying __proto__ keys. Attackers can pass untrusted JSON containing __proto__ or constructor.prototype payloads to merged objects, causing property injection, authorization bypass, or denial of service.

'@oleksii-pavlov/deep-merge before 1.2.4 contains a prototype pollution vulnerability in deepMergeTwoAssignable() that allows remote attackers to modify Object.prototype by supplying a __proto__ key. Attackers can pass JSON-parsed input to deepMerge(), deepMergeAndAssign(), deepUpdate() or deepUpdateAndAssign() to inject inherited properties, causing logic bypass or denial of service.

merge-deep-composed through 0.1.4 contains a prototype pollution vulnerability in _mergeDeepOne() that allows remote attackers to modify Object.prototype by supplying __proto__ keys. Attackers can pass JSON-parsed input containing __proto__ as a merge source to inject inherited properties, causing logic bypass or denial of service in Node.js processes.

build-git-clone before 1.0.4 contains an OS command injection vulnerability in the clone() function that allows attackers to execute commands by supplying crafted repository URLs. Attackers can embed shell metacharacters such as ; or $() in the url argument, which is concatenated into a sh -c command, to execute operating system commands with Node.js process privileges.

EverOS before 1.8.0 contains a cross-origin local file disclosure vulnerability that allows malicious websites to read local files by abusing a wildcard CORS policy with credentials and unrestricted file:// ingestion. Attackers can host JavaScript that calls POST /api/v2/memory/add with file:// URIs, then read parsed contents via POST /api/v2/memory/search to exfiltrate SSH keys, credentials, and alter or delete memories.

Assimp before 6.0.6 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in MD5Importer::MakeDataUnique() that allows attackers to corrupt heap memory by supplying unvalidated face indices. Attackers can craft an .md5mesh file with out-of-range face vertex indices or unfilled faces to set bits past the abHad allocation, read vertex data out of bounds, or crash the application.

Assimp before 6.0.6 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in MD5Importer::LoadMD5MeshFile() that allows attackers to corrupt heap memory via unvalidated weight ranges and bone indices. Attackers can supply a crafted .md5mesh file with out-of-range mBone values to increment heap words past the piCount allocation, causing memory corruption, out-of-bounds reads, or crashes.

Grav Form plugin before 9.2.4 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows page authors to write uploads into Twig template folders by setting an unchecked file field destination in Form::uploadFiles(). Attackers can upload .txt or .svg files containing Twig and have them rendered as trusted templates outside the sandbox, executing code as the web server user.

Grav Admin plugin before 1.10.65 contains a password reset poisoning vulnerability in LoginController::taskForgot() that ignores the Require Trusted Host setting when building reset links. Unauthenticated attackers who know an administrator's username can submit the forgot-password form with a forged Host header, capturing the reset token when clicked to take over accounts.

wpa_supplicant 2.7 through 2.12 with the wolfSSL backend contains an EAP-FAST server authentication bypass in tls_sess_sec_cb() that skips master secret derivation for oversized PAC-Opaque tickets. Adjacent attackers running a rogue authenticator can complete the handshake with an all-zero master secret to capture MS-CHAPv2 responses for offline cracking and replace the stored PAC.

markdownify-mcp before 1.2.0 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass URL validation by supplying DNS names, bracketed IPv6 literals, or IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. Attackers can influence URLs passed to webpage-to-markdown or git-repo-to-markdown through prompt injection to fetch loopback services, internal hosts, and cloud metadata endpoints.

Friendica through 2026.05-1 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability in item_edit() that allows authenticated local users to edit other authors' posts by submitting their own stored copy's post_id. Attackers can POST to /item to delete attachments and overwrite the shared body, title and content warning, which is shown under the original author's name.

A vulnerability was identified in SourceCodester Online Food Ordering System 1.0. Affected by this vulnerability is an unknown functionality of the file admin/partials/user_logged.php. The manipulation leads to missing authorization. Remote exploitation of the attack is possible. The exploit is publicly available and might be used.

ICU4C through 79.1 contains a use-after-free and double free vulnerability in the x11-compound-text converter because cloning shares the extraInfo block without a safeClone handler. Attackers who control the charset name passed to ucnv_open() in applications calling ucnv_setSubstString() or cloning converters can corrupt the heap, causing crashes and potentially code execution.

GNU mtools through 4.0.50 contains a divide-by-zero vulnerability that allows attackers to crash mtools commands by supplying a FAT image with a zero sectors-per-cluster byte. Attackers can craft a FAT image that, when opened with mdir, minfo or mtype, triggers a SIGFPE in calc_num_clus() on x86, causing denial of service.

A flaw was found in p11-kit. The RPC message attribute parsing functions p11_rpc_message_get_attribute() and p11_rpc_message_get_attribute_array_value() form a mutually-recursive call chain with no recursion depth limit when processing nested CKA_WRAP_TEMPLATE, CKA_UNWRAP_TEMPLATE, and CKA_DERIVE_TEMPLATE attributes. An unauthenticated attacker with local access to the p11-kit RPC Unix domain socket can send a specially crafted request with deeply nested template attributes, causing stack exhaustion and crashing the p11-kit server process and its dependent services.

A double free issue has been identified in libarchive's RAR5 reader. During parsing of a specially crafted RAR5 archive, the filtered_buf pointer may remain stale after being freed during unpacking state reinitialization. Subsequent processing of another archive entry can trigger a second free of the same memory region, resulting in a double-free condition. Successful exploitation may cause applications using the vulnerable libarchive API to terminate unexpectedly, leading to a denial of service.

A flaw was found in the ChunkReader component of the Undertow HTTP server, which is used by WildFly and JBoss EAP to handle chunked transfer encoding. The issue occurs because the parser uses a single internal variable to store both the remaining chunk size and state flags. By sending a specially crafted request with an extremely large chunk size, an attacker can cause these values to overlap, tricking the parser into thinking a request has finished prematurely. This can allow a second, "smuggled" request to be processed out of sync, potentially bypassing security controls.
RAOP module accepts unbounded Content-Length values and does not check the pw_array_add() return.
Multiple unbounded alloca() calls in the PulseAudio protocol server.

Use of externally-controlled format string vulnerability exists in RTU500 component of the logging function for TLS, PPP and CAM. Exploiting this vulnerability may result in sensitive memory disclosure and denial of service.

Two off-by-one errors in the FreeIPA ipa-otpd daemon's OAuth2 device authorization handler can cause out-of-bounds memory access when processing an oversized response from a configured external OAuth2/OIDC Identity Provider. An attacker who controls or can man-in-the-middle the IdP endpoint may be able to trigger ipa-otpd to write or read one byte past the end of a fixed-size buffer. Exploitation requires FreeIPA to be configured with an external IdP, attacker control or MITM of that IdP, and a user to initiate the OAuth2 device authorization flow. The most likely impact is limited denial of service affecting the ipa-otpd daemon.

A flaw was found in libsoup, an HTTP client library. This vulnerability, known as CRLF (Carriage Return Line Feed) Injection, occurs when an HTTP proxy is configured and the library improperly handles URL-decoded input used to create the Host header. A remote attacker can exploit this by providing a specially crafted URL containing CRLF sequences, allowing them to inject additional HTTP headers or complete HTTP request bodies. This can lead to unintended or unauthorized HTTP requests being forwarded by the proxy, potentially impacting downstream services.

A flaw was found in the GLib Base64 encoding routine when processing very large input data. Due to incorrect use of integer types during length calculation, the library may miscalculate buffer boundaries. This can cause memory writes outside the allocated buffer. Applications that process untrusted or extremely large Base64 input using GLib may crash or behave unpredictably.

A flaw was found in Glib's content type parsing logic. This buffer underflow vulnerability occurs because the length of a header line is stored in a signed integer, which can lead to integer wraparound for very large inputs. This results in pointer underflow and out-of-bounds memory access. Exploitation requires a local user to install or process a specially crafted treemagic file, which can lead to local denial of service or application instability.

A flaw was found in GLib. An integer overflow vulnerability in its Unicode case conversion implementation can lead to memory corruption. By processing specially crafted and extremely large Unicode strings, an attacker could trigger an undersized memory allocation, resulting in out-of-bounds writes. This could cause applications utilizing GLib for string conversion to crash or become unstable.

A logic vulnerability was found in GStreamer's webrtcbin component. The _check_sdp_crypto() function contains an inverted boolean condition that causes it to accept remote SDP offers or answers that lack the required a=fingerprint attribute, while incorrectly rejecting those that include it. An attacker with the ability to intercept and modify WebRTC signaling messages could exploit this to bypass the SDP-level DTLS certificate fingerprint binding, weakening defenses against man-in-the-middle attacks on media streams.

A heap-buffer-overflow flaw was found in 389 Directory Server (389-ds-base). When
normalizing a Distinguished Name (DN) that contains a legacy-quoted value encoding a
multivalued nested Relative Distinguished Name (RDN), the server can write past the
end of a heap allocation while sorting RDN attribute-value pairs. An unauthenticated
remote attacker can trigger this condition by sending an LDAP operation whose DN
reaches the DN normalization routine, such as a search with a crafted base DN. This
can corrupt heap memory and may cause denial of service.

A flaw was found in 389-ds-base where the LDBM backend attribute encryption uses a hardcoded static initialization vector for AES-CBC and 3DES-CBC operations, allowing an attacker with privileged filesystem access to detect plaintext equality across encrypted entries by comparing ciphertext blocks.

A flaw was found in the GNU Binutils (Binary Utilities) linker. This vulnerability, a heap-buffer-overflow read (CWE-125), occurs when the linker processes a specially crafted 32-bit XCOFF (Extended Common Object File Format) object file. An attacker could exploit this by providing a malicious file, leading to an out-of-bounds read of memory. This can result in information disclosure, potentially revealing sensitive heap data, and a Denial of Service (DoS) due to the linker crashing.

A flaw was found in libarchive. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to trigger a heap overflow by providing a specially crafted tar archive. The issue occurs during the parsing of a PAX extended header containing a malformed SUN.holesdata sparse-file attribute. Successful exploitation could lead to a denial of service, making the system unavailable, or potentially allow for arbitrary code execution, giving the attacker control over the affected system.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. The PBKDF2-SHA256 password verification function uses standard memcmp() for comparing password hashes instead of a constant-time comparison function. A remote attacker could potentially use timing measurements of LDAP bind attempts to infer partial hash information, though practical exploitation is extremely difficult due to PBKDF2 computational overhead.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by modifying the organization ID and target email within a legitimate invitation token's JSON Web Token (JWT) payload. This lack of cryptographic signature verification allows the attacker to successfully self-register into an unauthorized organization, leading to unauthorized access.

A flaw was found in fog-kubevirt. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to perform a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack due to disabled certificate validation. This enables the attacker to intercept and potentially alter sensitive communications between Satellite and OpenShift, resulting in information disclosure and data integrity compromise.

A flaw was found in foreman_kubevirt. When configuring the connection to OpenShift, the system disables SSL verification if a Certificate Authority (CA) certificate is not explicitly set. This insecure default allows a remote attacker, capable of intercepting network traffic between Satellite and OpenShift, to perform a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack. Such an attack could lead to the disclosure or alteration of sensitive information.

A flaw was found in libsoup. An attacker who can control the input for the Content-Disposition header can inject CRLF (Carriage Return Line Feed) sequences into the header value. These sequences are then interpreted verbatim when the HTTP request or response is constructed, allowing arbitrary HTTP headers to be injected. This vulnerability can lead to HTTP header injection or HTTP response splitting without requiring authentication or user interaction.

A flaw was found in libssh. During SFTP server directory listing, the longname field is constructed with unsafe concatenation into a fixed-size stack buffer. When a client causes the server to list attacker-controlled filenames, sufficiently long names can overflow that stack buffer and may lead to crashes or possible code execution on the server.

A flaw was found in the libsoup HTTP library that can cause proxy authentication credentials to be sent to unintended destinations. When handling HTTP redirects, libsoup removes the Authorization header but does not remove the Proxy-Authorization header if the request is redirected to a different host. As a result, sensitive proxy credentials may be leaked to third-party servers. Applications using libsoup for HTTP communication may unintentionally expose proxy authentication data.

Wildfly's IIOP listener may permit deserialization of input streams before authentication is performed. An attacker who can gain access to the IIOP port may be able to construct and send malicious objects and achieve deserialization, if the target EJB allows untyped method parameters, and depending on the potential gadget chains available in the running classpath.

A denial-of-service and resource exhaustion vulnerability exists within the `GDBus` component of GLib. The `gdbusauth` authentication mechanism fails to enforce proper length limitations on data lines read from a client. An unauthenticated local or remote attacker can exploit this lack of input validation by sending excessively long streams of data, causing the application to consume massive amounts of system memory and CPU, potentially leading to a crash or system hang.

A flaw was found in libsoup's WebSocket implementation when using the permessage-deflate extension. The extension's decompression loop (inflate()) processes data in chunks without enforcing an upper boundary limit on the output buffer size. While libsoup limits the incoming compressed frame size via max_incoming_payload_size, it fails to track or limit memory allocation during decompression. A separate check for decompressed size (max_total_message_size) exists but executes only after inflation is complete, and it is entirely disabled by default for client connections. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this by sending a small, highly compressed payload (a decompression bomb), causing unbounded memory allocation that triggers an Out-of-Memory (OOM) crash and a Denial of Service (DoS).

A heap buffer over-read vulnerability was discovered in libsoup's (versions: libsoup 3.0 to 3.7.0) HTTP/2 connection tracking framework. When the library processes an HTTP/2 GOAWAY frame, it improperly handles the "Additional Debug Data" payload by assuming the data stream is a safely NUL-terminated C-string. Because the parser lacks strict length-boundary verification before reading this data, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can intentionally send a malformed GOAWAY frame missing the appropriate null delimiter. This causes the library to read past the end of the allocated buffer, triggering an application crash that results in a denial of service (DoS), or potentially exposing fragments of memory contents.

A vulnerability was found in libsoup's HTTP/2 protocol implementation. The library fails to correctly release memory context blocks under specific stream termination conditions, such as when an HTTP/2 connection encounters window exhaustion or explicit stream resets. A remote, unauthenticated attacker acting as a malicious network peer can trick the connection engine into allocating stream states that are subsequently leaked during cleanup. Over a sustained period, this flaw allows the remote attacker to consume the system's heap allocations incrementally, triggering a denial of service (DoS) through an ultimate Out-of-Memory (OOM) application crash.

An out-of-bounds read vulnerability was found in libsoup's multipart processing subsystem. The flaw exists in the soup_multipart_input_stream_read_headers() function inside soup-multipart-input-stream.c, which does not adequately restrict or validate the size of incoming multipart boundary strings. When processing a crafted HTTP response containing a malformed or oversized boundary parameter, the internal stream reader reads past the allocated buffer bounds. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this behavior to cause a service denial (DoS) through application failure or potentially read fragments of unauthorized memory metadata.

A flaw was found in samba's pam_winbind. When mkhomedir is enabled, pam_winbind chowns the target account's home directory without validating the path is not a critical system directory such as /. On affected systems, accounts with / as their home directory (a common default for system accounts) can have this triggered not only by root, but by a non-root user holding a narrow sudo delegation to run commands as that account, causing ownership of / to change and resulting in severe denial of service (SSH, sudo, and package-manager failures). The change does not grant write access to / (which ships with restrictive 0555 permissions on RHEL), so the impact is availability loss rather than further privilege escalation.

A vulnerability was found in kronosnet's (version <=1.34) cryptographic configuration management. The framework does not correctly zero-out or wipe sensitive memory segments after executing changes to its cryptographic configuration. This omission leaves raw encryption keys resident in memory after the associated structures are freed. A local attacker capable of leveraging memory disclosure techniques could exploit this flaw to retrieve the active encryption key, allowing them to decrypt cluster network communications or inject malicious packets to cause severe high-availability cluster instability.

A vulnerability was found in the internal Access Control List (ACL) subsystem of kronosnet (Version affected: <= 1.34). When the framework is explicitly configured to manage dynamic links (accepting network traffic from any IP address) without network payload encryption, the validation architecture implicitly trusts the link ID provided within incoming data packets. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this lack of validation by spoofing a legitimate link ID inside crafted network frames. This allows the attacker to fully bypass the ACL framework and inject arbitrary data packets into the application layer, potentially leading to data corruption or service instabilities.

A vulnerability was found in the network packet de-fragmentation engine of kronosnet (Version affected <= 1.34). The internal reassembly code does not properly validate sequence numbers of incoming payload fragments. An attacker can exploit this lack of verification by transmitting malformed packets with corrupted sequence parameters. Under specific conditions, this forces the packet processing layer to parse data outside the designated bounds of the internal memory structures, causing an out-of-bounds memory access or heap corruption. This behavior can result in sudden application crashes or system instability.

Ivanti Endpoint Manager (EPM) contains an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to leak specific stored credential data.

A flaw was found in xdgmime. A heap-based buffer overflow can be triggered in _xdg_mime_magic_parse_magic_line() in the xdgmimemagic.c file on little-endian systems when an attacker-controlled MIME magic file in a user-writable XDG data location (e.g., in the $XDG_DATA_HOME/mime/magic path) is parsed by an application performing MIME type detection (e.g., via g_content_type_guess()). When performing byte-swap, incorrect pointer arithmetic on the write side causes an out-of-bounds write of 2 bytes, resulting in an application crash or memory corruption.

A stack-based buffer overflow was found in rpcbind's rpcinfo utility. When querying a remote rpcbind service with `rpcinfo -l`, address information returned by the server is copied into a fixed-size buffer without sufficient bounds checking. A malicious or compromised rpcbind server could use this flaw to crash the rpcinfo client, resulting in a denial of service. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

A stack-based buffer overflow was found in rpcbind's rpcinfo utility. In rpcbdump() short mode (used by `rpcinfo -s`), version numbers from a remote RPCBPROC_DUMP reply are written into a fixed-size stack buffer without bounds checking. A user or administrator who runs `rpcinfo -s` against a malicious or compromised rpcbind endpoint could experience a crash or denial of service of the rpcinfo client.

A flaw was found in the sbc library (BlueZ SBC codec). An off-by-one error in the SBC frame decoder allows a crafted audio payload to trigger a one-byte heap out-of-bounds read. This could allow an adjacent attacker streaming Bluetooth audio to read a single byte of adjacent heap memory.

A signed integer overflow vulnerability was found in libarchive's ZIP writer. In the archive_write_zip_header function in archive_write_set_format_zip.c, when ZIP encryption is enabled and the entry file size is close to INT64_MAX, the addition of the encryption overhead to the entry size overflows int64_t, resulting in undefined behavior. This could lead to incorrect Zip64 extension decisions or potential memory corruption.

A flaw was found in the PCP (Performance Co-Pilot) `pmproxy` service. A remote attacker can exploit a vulnerability in the `pmLogLoadInDom()` function by sending a specially crafted request. This bypasses a critical bounds check, which can lead to the `pmproxy` service crashing, causing a Denial of Service (DoS). Additionally, this flaw may enable the leakage of sensitive information from the system's memory.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit a path traversal vulnerability in the PCP pmproxy logger servlet using a crafted hostname. This allows arbitrary file and directory creation, potentially leading to a denial of service.

A heap-buffer-overflow flaw was found in Directory Server (389-ds-base). When a DN contains a legacy-quoted value, the server won't close the heap allocation allowing another call to refer to the same memory pointer causing a denial of service or an arbitrary memory write operation.

MCUboot's encrypted serial-recovery path contains an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds stack write in decrypt_region_inplace() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c. The routine decrypts an uploaded encrypted image one flash sector at a time into a sector-sized stack VLA buf[sz], but when the current sector is still inside the image header it sets the destination index to the absolute header size (idx = hdr->ih_hdr_size; at boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:156) and then decrypts into &buf[idx]. The correct sibling routine boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:876 uses the sector-relative idx = hdr->ih_hdr_size - abs_off; the serial path is missing the - abs_off term, so for any sector after the first the index runs past the end of the stack buffer.

The ih_hdr_size field is a uint16_t taken verbatim from the uploaded image header. On the second sector onward, when ih_hdr_size exceeds the sector size, &buf[idx] points beyond buf and boot_enc_decrypt() writes attacker-controlled plaintext into adjacent stack frames. The path is reached pre-authentication: bs_upload() calls boot_handle_enc_fw() (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c:1208) after upload, and the pre-decryption signature gate in decrypt_image_inplace() is compiled out (#if 0 at boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:226-233), so the header is never validated before decryption.

A second error in the same window computation affects the first sector. When a sector holds both the end of the header and the start of the TLV area, the decrypt length is clamped to tlv_off - (off + bytes_copied), measured from the start of the sector rather than from idx (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:166). An encrypted image whose header and payload end within the first sector is therefore decrypted for ih_hdr_size bytes more than it should be: into the TLV area and, when the image ends near the end of the sector, past buf. This form needs no oversized header, so even an ordinary small encrypted image can trigger it, and it reaches devices with sectors of up to about 128 KiB rather than only those whose sector is smaller than the 16-bit ih_hdr_size.

Reaching the sink requires a build with MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES and serial recovery enabled, and access to the device's serial/USB recovery interface (unauthenticated by design). With the public-key encryption schemes the AES content key is wrapped to the device's public encryption key, so an attacker can author a fully crafted encrypted image — including a malicious ih_hdr_size — without the image-signing private key. The result is a controllable stack memory-corruption inside the bootloader before any signature check, providing a path to code execution in the secure-boot root of trust that bypasses image authentication, as well as a denial-of-service. A 2048-byte out-of-bounds write was reproduced under AddressSanitizer (sz=4096, off=4096, ih_hdr_size=6144).

On releases before v2.0.0 (v1.9.0 and v1.10.0) the destination is a file-scope static uint8_t buf[SOC_FLASH_ERASE_BLK_SZ] in .bss rather than the stack VLA described above — the code then lived in boot/zephyr/single_loader.c, before commit c9fa6088 relocated it to boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c and changed the buffer's storage class. The out-of-bounds write is equally real and equally pre-authentication on those releases, but it corrupts adjacent static data rather than the stack, so a stack-smashing proof of concept written against a current release will not reproduce as-is there.

Summary

MCUboot enforces several security-critical invariants on the boot, image-swap, and validation paths using assert(). In a standard release/production build (NDEBUG defined) assert() expands to a no-op, so an invariant the code intends to halt on instead falls through, and execution continues with the bad or inconsistent state. Where the guarded condition is attacker-influenceable through the flash-write boundary (serial-recovery / DFU), this is a security check that is simply absent in release builds.

This is one root cause (assert-as-security-guard, no-op under NDEBUG) with one fix approach (replace the security-critical asserts with real fail-closed checks), so it is filed as a single advisory covering the enumerated sites.

Worst reachable instance — inconsistent swap status completes the swap without validation

In the swap-resume status read, an inconsistent status (erased_sections > 1) is detected, logged, and — when MCUBOOT_VALIDATE_PRIMARY_SLOT is disabled — is meant to abort, because "there is no way to be sure the swapped primary slot is OK." The abort is assert(0):

boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c:181-194 — if (erased_sections > 1) { ... #if !defined(MCUBOOT_VALIDATE_PRIMARY_SLOT) / ... abort! / assert(0); #endif }, then execution falls through to compute bs->op/idx/state from the inconsistent status (lines 197-208) and return 0 (success).
boot/bootutil/src/swap_offset.c:266-280 — identical pattern; falls through to bs->op/idx/state and return 0.
boot/bootutil/src/swap_scratch.c:227-241 — same invalid/assert(0) pattern for the scratch backend.

Under NDEBUG with primary-slot validation off, the inconsistent status is neither aborted (assert is a no-op) nor re-validated (validation off), so boot_complete_partial_swap() finishes the swap on inconsistent metadata and the primary slot is booted without a signature check. An attacker who can write the swap-status trailer can craft the inconsistent status.

Reachability (threat model). Secondary slot + scratch trailers are A2-writable by definition (that is what a DFU upload is). Under MCUBOOT_SERIAL_RECOVERY the primary trailer is A2-writable too: boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c:978 opens flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot(img_num, 0) (== primary) and writes from offset 0 bounded by area_size, so it can paint the primary swap-status/magic. This is how the A2 (recovery/DFU, unauthenticated by design) attacker influences the guarded condition. Property violated: P1 (image authenticity / secure-boot bypass) when un-revalidated content is booted, and P6 (boot/recovery availability).

Second reachable instance — resume-path swap_size from an unguarded trailer

boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:1190-1193: the swap resume branch does fap = boot_find_status(...); assert(fap != NULL); rc = boot_read_swap_size(fap, &bs->swap_size); assert(rc == 0);. boot_find_status() (boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_misc.c:166-204) searches {scratch, primary} and, on no-valid-magic-match, returns the last-iterated area (primary), not NULL — so assert(fap != NULL) cannot fire even in debug, and under NDEBUG neither assert fires. swap_size is then read from an A2-writable (serial-recovery primary, or scratch) trailer with no fail-closed handling. This is the same swap-metadata-trust family as the recorded resume/swap_size disclosure.

Reachable-security sites (center the fix here)

1. boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c:193 — inconsistent-status assert(0), falls through to complete swap. A2 + !VALIDATE_PRIMARY. [worst]
2. boot/bootutil/src/swap_offset.c:278 — same, swap-offset backend.
3. boot/bootutil/src/swap_scratch.c:239 — same, swap-scratch backend.
4. boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:1191 and :1193 — resume assert(fap != NULL) / assert(rc == 0) guarding swap_size read from an A2-writable trailer; compounded by boot_find_status() never returning NULL.

When MCUboot resumes an interrupted image swap it takes the number of bytes to move straight from the flash-resident status trailer. In boot_swap_image() (boot/bootutil/src/loader.c) the fresh-swap branch recomputes copy_size from the image headers and is bounded — swap_run() in boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c carries an explicit "not enough free space" check (last_idx >= first_trailer_idx) — but that check runs only inside if (boot_status_is_reset(bs)). On the resume branch the code instead does boot_read_swap_size(fap, &bs->swap_size); copy_size = bs->swap_size; and passes the value to swap_run() with no re-derivation and no bound.

swap_run() turns that byte count into a sector index by summing sector sizes until it reaches the count, with no ceiling on the real sector count: find_last_idx() in swap_move.c and swap_offset.c, and find_last_sector_idx() in swap_scratch.c, are all while (1) loops. The resulting index is fed to boot_img_sector_off() / boot_img_sector_size() (boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_priv.h), which index the fixed BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS sectors[] arrays with no bounds check. Past num_sectors the loop reads zero-initialised — and past BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS, adjacent-struct — entries; a sector size of 0 makes the loop never terminate, and a bogus computed offset is handed to boot_erase_region() / boot_copy_region() as an out-of-bounds flash erase or copy.

MCUboot itself only ever writes a validated, slot-bounded swap_size (swap_misc.c, fixup_revert()), so reaching the defect requires writing the trailer from outside. Serial recovery provides exactly that: an upload writes attacker bytes contiguously from offset 0 of the primary slot (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c, via flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot()), bounded only by img_size <= area_size, so it controls the whole trailer — magic, swap_info, op/idx/state and swap_size. The resume gate boot_status_is_reset() keys solely on those op/idx/state fields, and boot_find_status() explicitly trusts valid magic as implying valid metadata. A forged in-progress status with an oversized swap_size therefore drives the unbounded walk during swap setup — before the primary image's signature is validated, and serial recovery is unauthenticated by design.

The outcome is an out-of-bounds flash erase or copy, or a non-terminating loop, inside the bootloader: an unbootable or bricked device, with the possibility of bootloader memory corruption. That exceeds what serial recovery is designed to grant, which is only the ability to stage an image that must still pass signature verification.

Exposure requires a swap-based update backend — MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_MOVE (the default for swap builds), MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_SCRATCH or MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_OFFSET; overwrite-only, direct-XIP and RAM-load builds are unaffected — together with MCUBOOT_SERIAL_RECOVERY. Without serial recovery the path is only reachable by an attacker who can already write flash directly, which is outside the threat model.

The fix is to treat the trailer's swap_size as untrusted: reject or clamp it in boot_swap_image() before it becomes copy_size, bounding it by the primary slot's usable image area (sector count x sector size, excluding the trailer) rather than the raw flash_area_get_size(), and aborting recovery with a non-zero error on overflow. The same guard should cover the independent boot_read_swap_size() reads in each backend's boot_read_image_header().

The Cypress/PSoC6 flash-map backend in boot/cypress/cy_flash_pal/cy_flash_map.c guards every flash access with assert() against the wrong struct field. flash_area_read(), flash_area_write(), and flash_area_erase() check assert(off < fa->fa_off) and assert(off + len < fa->fa_off), comparing the area-relative off against the partition's absolute base address fa->fa_off instead of its length fa->fa_size. Because fa_off is a large absolute address, realistic out-of-partition offsets pass the check even in a debug build, and under NDEBUG the asserts are removed entirely. The access then proceeds as memcpy() (or a flash row op) at fa->fa_off + off with no enforcement.

The MCUboot core does not bound image-region offsets itself; it relies on flash_area_read() returning an error. During pre-authentication image validation, bootutil_img_hash() in boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_img_hash.c loops over ih_hdr_size + ih_img_size + ih_protect_tlv_size — all attacker-controlled header fields of the still-unverified update image — calling flash_area_read(), and the TLV iterator in boot/bootutil/src/tlv.c reads attacker-derived offsets the same way. An attacker who can stage a crafted image in the secondary/update slot (via OTA, DFU, or serial recovery, depending on the product) declares an oversized ih_img_size, causing reads far past the partition. A correct backend would reject these and fail validation cleanly; the Cypress backend does not.

The out-of-bounds access is in the source address of the copy — the destination buffer is correctly sized — so there is no memory corruption, no information disclosure to the attacker (the data is only folded into a hash that still fails the signature check), and no authentication bypass. The realistic impact is a bus fault or hang when the computed absolute address lands on an unmapped or peripheral region of the PSoC6 address map: the bootloader crashes instead of rejecting the bad image, an availability (denial-of-service) impact. The defect is specific to the Cypress/PSoC6 port; mainline Zephyr/sim/mynewt backends are unaffected. The identical broken guard in the write/erase primitives is a latent out-of-bounds-write gap, but no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds offset was found to reach those (serial-recovery uploads are bounded by the core), so the reachable memory-safety bug is the out-of-bounds read.

The vendored zcbor decoder's zcbor_any_skip() in boot/zcbor/src/zcbor_decode.c descends one C-stack frame per level of CBOR nesting. On a list or map it copies the decoder state (memcpy(&state_copy, state, sizeof(zcbor_state_t))) and recurses once per member, with no depth cap: the skip path does not use zcbor's backup stack, and ZCBOR_MAX_ELEM_COUNT is SIZE_MAX, so nothing bounds how deep the recursion goes.

That function is reached on attacker-controlled bytes before any authentication. MCUboot's serial-recovery command parser decodes SMP/CBOR requests with zcbor_map_decode_bulk() (boot/boot_serial/src/zcbor_bulk.c), which skips any map key it does not recognise by calling zcbor_any_skip() on the encoded value; the echo handler in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c calls it directly on the same footing. Both run during image upload, long before the uploaded image's signature is checked. The default receive buffer is MCUBOOT_SERIAL_MAX_RECEIVE_SIZE = 512 bytes and each nesting level costs a single byte to encode (0x81), so roughly 500 levels of nesting fit in one request — comfortably more than a bootloader's stack can absorb, since every frame carries a full zcbor_state_t copy plus locals.

The impact is availability only: the bootloader's stack overflows and the device faults or hangs during recovery. There is no controlled out-of-bounds write that escapes the DFU buffer, no disclosure, and no authentication bypass — the recursion grows the stack with the decoder's own internal state. Whether a given board actually exhausts its stack depends on that board's bootloader stack size, which we did not measure; the fix is nevertheless unconditional, because an unauthenticated pre-authentication code path must not have its safety depend on a per-board stack margin.

Exposure requires MCUBOOT_SERIAL (serial/SMP recovery), which is not enabled by default, and recovery entry is normally gated on a physical pin (CONFIG_BOOT_SERIAL_ENTRANCE_GPIO / PIN_RESET), with a no-valid-image fallback path. Products that expose serial recovery over an externally reachable transport, or that fall into recovery when no valid image is present, are the ones at risk.

The fix is to bound the skip: thread a recursion-depth counter through zcbor_any_skip() (or have zcbor_map_decode_bulk() reject values nested beyond a small constant) and fail once the limit is exceeded — equivalently, take the bounded-skip implementation from upstream zcbor.

MCUboot's Espressif port omits zeroization of two sensitive stack buffers in boot/espressif/hal/src/flash_encrypt.c. In check_and_generate_encryption_keys(), the freshly generated XTS-AES flash-encryption key is held in the stack array keys[BLOCKS_NEEDED][32] (flash_encrypt.c:216), written to eFuse via esp_efuse_write_keys(), and the function returns (flash_encrypt.c:243) without scrubbing it. In esp_flash_encrypt_region(), the plaintext flash sector buffer buf (flash_encrypt.c:454) retains the last sector's cleartext at both the success and flash_failed returns. Neither path performs a memset/bzero/mbedtls_platform_zeroize, even though the same port already does bzero for key digests in boot/espressif/hal/src/secure_boot.c.

The affected code runs only on the Espressif port with CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENC_ENABLED, and only during the one-time first-boot provisioning pass when flash encryption is not yet enabled (boot/espressif/main.c); on subsequent boots the buffers are never created. Recovering the residue requires an out-of-band stack/RAM-disclosure primitive — JTAG/debug halt, UART ROM download, a core/crash dump, or a warm-boot RAM scrape — captured during that single provisioning boot. Under the recommended CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENCRYPTION_MODE_RELEASE plus secure boot, those channels are fused off and no exposure exists.

The practical impact is a low-severity, defense-in-depth hardening gap: a flash-encryption key (and last plaintext sector) may linger in bootloader stack memory. Because the eFuse key block is burned read+write-protected, the transient stack copy is the only readable copy, and only during one boot; in a development build where a disclosure channel is open, an attacker with that capability can usually already read the still-plaintext flash directly, so the marginal confidentiality gain is small. Confirming real-world recovery depends on a specific SoC/debug configuration not exercisable from source alone.

MCUboot's PSA-crypto ECDSA adapter parses the RFC 5480 DER signature with parse_signature_from_rfc5480_encoding() in boot/bootutil/include/bootutil/crypto/ecdsa.h, which takes no length argument. bootutil_ecdsa_verify() explicitly discards the signature length ((void)slen;) and the parser walks the encoding using length bytes read from the buffer itself (r_len = sig[3], then a derived s_len), with no check that those offsets stay within the supplied signature. Because this parsing runs before psa_verify_hash(), a malformed signature triggers the read whether or not the signature is valid.

In bootutil_img_validate() (boot/bootutil/src/image_validate.c:404) the ECDSA signature TLV is gated only by len > sizeof(buf), since EXPECTED_SIG_LEN() is the constant 1 for ECDSA; len is attacker-controlled in the range 0..128 and is copied into the 128-byte stack buffer buf. With a crafted r_len (e.g. sig[3] = 255) the parser's memcpy reads roughly 130+ bytes past the end of buf, an out-of-bounds read of adjacent stack memory. Reaching the signature case only requires a key TLV that matches a trusted public key (public material), so the path is effectively pre-authentication.

The defect is gated to the PSA crypto backend (MCUBOOT_USE_PSA_CRYPTO) with MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC256/MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384 (and MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384 always builds with PSA); the in-tree CC310, TinyCrypt, and mbedTLS adapters use different decoders and are not affected. This is not a signature bypass: the over-read bytes feed a verification that fails closed and are never returned to the attacker, so there is no information leak. The impact is bounded to a possible fault/denial-of-service on memory layouts where the read crosses an unmapped region; on typical flat-memory MCUs it reads adjacent RAM without faulting.
This vulnerability was reported independently twice: by NVIDIA Project Vanessa on 2026-06-22, and by Kai Phan (@kaimandalic) on 2026-07-19 as GHSA-r44p-8v6p-hqv4, which is closed as a duplicate of this advisory. Both original reports are reproduced in full below. The second report additionally observes that bootutil_ecdsa_parse_public_key() discards its end pointer ((void)end;, ecdsa.h:446). That observation is correct, but it is not part of this vulnerability and is not counted in the severity: the buffer it parses is bootutil_keys[key_id].key, the compiled-in trusted key store (image_ecdsa.c:54-55), so no attacker-controlled data reaches that parse. It is a robustness gap on the same code path and should be closed alongside the signature-parser fix. Note also that the second report's proof-of-concept models the signature buffer as an 8-byte heap allocation and therefore reports a heap overflow; in MCUboot the buffer is the 128-byte stack array buf, gated by len > sizeof(buf), so the real over-read is of adjacent stack memory.

GitLab has remediated an issue in GitLab EE affecting all versions from 17.4 before 19.4.11, 19.5 before 19.5.9, and 19.6 before 19.6.2 that on instances with receptive cluster agents enabled could have allowed an authenticated user with Maintainer-role permissions to make requests to internal network services through the GitLab agent server due to insufficient validation of destination addresses.

A flaw was found in gdk-pixbuf. When parsing a specially crafted ICO file with pixel values that exceed the defined palette range, an out-of-bounds read can occur due to improper bounds checking against the actual palette size. This vulnerability causes heap bytes to be interpreted as valid palette indices and rendered as RGB pixel values in the output image, allowing an attacker to extract heap content via the generated output, such as a thumbnail.

A flaw was found in pki-core. The certificate authority (CA) renewal request path does not perform the realm-based authorization check that the enrollment path performs, allowing an authenticated user entitled to one realm to cause a certificate belonging to a different realm to be renewed without that realm's authorization.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-good. A heap-based out-of-bounds read of 4 bytes can occur when parsing FLAC audio stream headers embedded in a Matroska or WebM container file. The vulnerability is triggered by a boundary check that does not account for the full size of the data being copied, allowing a small read past the end of the allocated buffer. An attacker could exploit this by crafting a malicious Matroska or WebM file and tricking a user into opening it, potentially leaking a small amount of adjacent heap memory.

A flaw was found in CRI-O's container-creation environment-variable handling
(`mergeEnvs` in `server/utils.go`, consumed by `setupContainerEnvironmentAndWorkdir` in
`server/container_create.go`). When a `CreateContainer` request supplies a `nil` CRI
`Envs` field, CRI-O falls back to using the target OCI image's `config.Env` entries
unfiltered, in contrast to the normal merge path, which validates each entry for a
`key=value` form before use. An OCI image whose `config.Env` contains an entry with no
`=` character (e.g. a bare `NOEQUALS` string) causes CRI-O to split that entry into a
single-element slice and then index its second element, which is out of range. This
triggers an unrecovered Go runtime panic in the `crio` daemon process, crashing it and
terminating the container-runtime service for all workloads on the node until it is
restarted.

GitLab has remediated an issue in GitLab CE/EE affecting all versions from 16.7.0 before 19.4.11, 19.5 before 19.5.9, and 19.6 before 19.6.2 that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user with developer-role permissions to merge code changes into protected branches without triggering approval resets due to the use of a weak hash function in the merge request approval change detection mechanism.

BeyondTrust Remote Support (RS) and Privileged Remote Access (PRA)contain an OS command injection vulnerability. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute operating system commands in the context of the site user. Successful exploitation requires no authentication or user interaction and may lead to system compromise, including unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and service disruption.

A flaw was identified in the interactive shell of the xmllint utility, part of the libxml2 project, where memory allocated for user input is not properly released under certain conditions. When a user submits input consisting only of whitespace, the program skips command execution but fails to free the allocated buffer. Repeating this action causes memory to continuously accumulate. Over time, this can exhaust system memory and terminate the xmllint process, creating a denial-of-service condition on the local system.

A flaw was found in libarchive. An attacker can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) or potential information disclosure due to a use-after-free vulnerability, which occurs when a program reads memory that has already been released. This issue arises when the archive_entry_copy_mac_metadata() function deallocates an internal buffer before completing a data copy. An attacker who can supply input to an application utilizing this function can trigger the flaw to crash the application or read uninitialized memory data.

A flaw was found in SoupServer. This HTTP request smuggling vulnerability occurs because SoupServer improperly handles requests that combine Transfer-Encoding: chunked and Connection: keep-alive headers. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this by sending specially crafted requests, causing SoupServer to fail to close the connection as required by RFC 9112. This allows the attacker to smuggle additional requests over the persistent connection, leading to unintended request processing and potential denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.

A path traversal flaw was found in WildFly's domain mode
  implementation. The LocalFileRepository.getFile() and
  getConfigurationFile() methods in
  wildfly-core/deployment-repository do not validate that the
  resolved file path remains within the configured repository or
  configuration root directories. A remote attacker who has
  obtained the slave host controller secret or compromised a slave
  host controller can supply a crafted relative path containing
  directory traversal sequences (e.g., ../../etc/passwd) via the
  slave-DC wire protocol, causing the Domain Controller to resolve
  and serve arbitrary files readable by the DC process. This leads
  to unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information such as
  configuration files, keystores, and system credentials.

A flaw was found in RESTEasy's SourceProvider. This vulnerability allows an unauthenticated attacker to perform an unauthenticated remote file read. By sending a specially crafted XML body with a DOCTYPE declaration referencing external entities to an endpoint that accepts application/xml and returns Source or StreamSource, the server can be tricked into resolving the entity and including sensitive file contents in the HTTP response. This is due to the SourceProvider.writeTo() method creating a SAXParser without disabling external entity resolution, leading to an XML External Entity (XXE) vulnerability.

A flaw was found in libsoup, an HTTP client/server library. This HTTP Request Smuggling vulnerability arises from non-RFC-compliant parsing in the soup_filter_input_stream_read_line() logic, where libsoup accepts malformed chunk headers, such as lone line feed (LF) characters instead of the required carriage return and line feed (CRLF). A remote attacker can exploit this without authentication or user interaction by sending specially crafted chunked requests. This allows libsoup to parse and process multiple HTTP requests from a single network message, potentially leading to information disclosure.

A flaw was found in Dogtag PKI's ACME responder where the web.xml security constraints use exact URL pattern matching for admin-only enable/disable endpoints. By appending a trailing slash to the URL, an unauthenticated attacker can bypass the Tomcat authentication constraint while RESTEasy still routes the request to the handler, allowing unauthorized toggling of the ACME service state including persistent denial of service.

A flaw was found in gdk-pixbuf. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to cause a heap out-of-bounds read by providing a specially crafted Apple Icon Image (.icns) file. The uncompress() function, which handles RLE-encoded ICNS icon data, fails to validate the source buffer's boundaries during decompression. This can lead to a denial of service, where the application crashes, or to information disclosure, potentially revealing sensitive data from adjacent memory.

A flaw was found in dhcp-server. A remote attacker with network access to the OMAPI (Open Management Application Programming Interface) port, especially if not secured with TSIG (Transaction Signature) key authentication, could send a specially crafted lease creation request. This request, containing an overly long InfiniBand MAC address, triggers a buffer overflow in the `print_hw_addr()` function. Successful exploitation leads to a persistent denial of service (DoS), causing the `dhcpd` service to crash and preventing it from restarting without manual intervention.

A flaw was found in CRIU's handling of restartable sequences (rseq) during checkpoint/restore. A malicious process inside a container can register an rseq critical section that hijacks CRIU's parasite code injection during checkpoint, allowing it to spoof the process credentials saved in the checkpoint image. On restore, the container process gains elevated capabilities and zeroed UIDs/GIDs.

The practical impact on Red Hat products is limited by several factors: checkpoint/restore requires root privileges (podman) or cluster-admin RBAC (OpenShift) to trigger and cannot be initiated from within the container itself; on OpenShift prior to 4.17 the feature required explicit opt-in, and on 4.17+ the kubelet checkpoint API RBAC is not configured by default; OpenShift enforces user namespaces by default for regular workloads (hostUsers is gated behind admin-only SCCs), which makes the spoofed capabilities namespace-scoped and ineffective for privilege escalation; SELinux type enforcement (container_t) blocks privilege transitions independently of capabilities; seccomp filters persist through checkpoint/restore and cannot be corrupted via the parasite; and kernel mount namespace ownership checks on RHEL 9/10 kernels prevent mount-based container escape even with spoofed capabilities.

A flaw was found in gnome-remote-desktop as shipped in Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
