Description

The SQL status backend serialises per-URL metadata into a single column by concatenating a tabulation,
the key, an equals sign and the value, with no escaping. On read-back the string is split on the same
two characters, so the round trip is not injective: a value that contains a tabulation returns as one
or more additional keys that were never written.

Values on that path are supplied by crawled servers. `FetcherBolt` records the raw `Location` header of
a redirect as `_redirTo`, and `_redirTo` is part of the default `metadata.persist` set, so a redirect
whose `Location` contains a tabulation followed by `key=value` pairs introduces those keys into the
crawler's own control metadata on the next scheduling cycle. Several control keys are read without a
prefix, so the injected keys are live: `http.proxy.host`, `http.proxy.port`, `http.proxy.user` and
`http.proxy.pass` among them, as well as scheduling and request-shaping keys such as `depth`,
`max.depth`, `crawl.delay`, `http.content.limit` and `isSitemap`.

Where a proxy manager is configured, the consequence is not limited to corrupted scheduling data.
`SingleProxyManager.getProxy(Metadata)` consults the per-URL metadata first and returns what it finds,
so an injected proxy host and port take precedence over the operator's configured proxy and subsequent
fetches, together with any configured `Authorization` header, are routed through a host the crawled
content chose. A related defect in `AbstractStatusUpdaterBolt` compounds this: an injected
`status.store.as.is.with.nextfetchdate` that is not a valid instant escapes the enclosing try/catch and
stops the bolt, and because the stored row is replayed the failure repeats.

Deployments using the OpenSearch or Solr status backends are unaffected, because those serialise
metadata structurally.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where the metadata column is written in an escaped form behind a format marker, rows
written by earlier versions are still decoded unchanged, and the stored next-fetch-date is parsed
defensively.

The fix does not repair rows written before the upgrade. Operators using the SQL status backend should
inspect the metadata column of an existing status table for tabulation characters and remove the
affected rows, and should assume any proxy credentials configured for the crawl may have been exercised
through an attacker-chosen proxy and rotate them. Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove
`_redirTo` from `metadata.persist` to close the demonstrated path, though other crawled values reaching
persisted metadata remain.

Description

When StormCrawler fetches a host's `/robots.txt` and receives a redirect, `HttpRobotRulesParser`
resolves the `Location` header and re-fetches the target for up to five hops. The loop checks neither
the scheme, the host nor the port of the resolved target, and it is not governed by
`http.allow.redirects`, which only affects the page fetch. A crawled site can therefore point the
robots.txt fetch at any address reachable from the fetcher worker, including loopback interfaces,
private ranges and cloud metadata endpoints. Every crawled URL triggers a robots.txt fetch on a cache
miss, so no unusual configuration is required to reach the loop.

The fetched body is only parsed as robots rules and is not returned to the caller, so the read itself
is blind. The more direct impact is on credentials: the okhttp protocol applies its configured request
headers, including the `Authorization` header built from `http.basicauth.user` and
`http.basicauth.password` and anything in `http.custom.headers`, to every request it makes. Because
StormCrawler follows the redirect itself and issues a new request, okhttp's own removal of the
`Authorization` header across a host change does not apply, and the operator's crawl credentials are
delivered to the host the redirect names.

The connection-time IP filter, `http.filter.ipaddress.include` and `http.filter.ipaddress.exclude`, is
installed as an okhttp network interceptor on the same client and does apply to these hops when it is
configured. It ships with no rules, which is why the path is reachable in a default configuration. URL
filtering never applies, because the robots.txt fetch does not pass through the outlink filter chain.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where a robots.txt redirect is followed only when the target uses http or https and
shares scheme, host and port with the URL it was reached from. Deployments that legitimately serve
robots.txt through a cross-host redirect can restore the previous behaviour with
`http.robots.redirect.crosshost.allow`.

Any authenticated account, including self-registered or zero-rights users, can exploit this flaw to gain read, write, and delete access to the OpenSearch cluster.

openIMIS before 2026-10 contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the core export mixin (openimis-be-core_py, core/gql/export_mixin.py) that allows authenticated users with a single ordinary read right to traverse arbitrary foreign key relations by supplying caller-controlled dotted field paths that are rewritten into Django ORM syntax without an allow-list. Attackers can exploit this to export another user's JWT signing key via a path such as user_created.i_user.private_key, enabling them to forge valid authenticated sessions for other accounts, including administrators, without detection through failed-login events or invalidation by password reset.

openIMIS before 2026-10 contains an improper validation vulnerability in the deduplication service (openimis-be-deduplication_py, deduplication/services.py) that allows a caller holding only the narrow right 170001 to bypass column path validation by exploiting the fact that only the first segment of a dotted relation path is checked before the full unvalidated path is used in the query. Attackers can supply a crafted dotted column path such as user_created__i_user__private_key to traverse relations and retrieve an administrator's JWT signing key, enabling forgery of a valid administrator session without a password that survives password resets and generates no failed-login event.

openIMIS before 2026-10 contains a remote code execution vulnerability in the report module's overrideReport GraphQL mutation, which stores submitted report definitions without proper validation before rendering them with the simpleeval expression evaluator. An attacker holding only limited report add, edit, or query privileges can craft a printIf expression that leverages the datetime module to reach os.system functions, bypassing the name-prefix blocklist to execute arbitrary operating-system commands as root whenever the malicious report is later rendered by any viewer, including administrators or scheduled jobs.

openIMIS before 2026-10 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the FHIR R4 module (openimis-be-api_fhir_r4_py) that allows an authenticated attacker with limited district-level access to receive subscription notifications for data outside their authorized scope due to the absence of row-level security checks such as has_perms, get_queryset, ROW_SECURITY, district, or health-facility scoping on the notification delivery path. Attackers can register a standing FHIR subscription to continuously receive claim data and can further direct notification pushes to internal network addresses.

openIMIS before 2026-10 contains a broken access control vulnerability in the FHIR R4 module that allows any authenticated attacker to delete Coverage policy records due to an empty permissions_delete list being vacuously granted by user.has_perms([]). Attackers can issue a DELETE request to the Coverage/<uuid>/ endpoint to permanently and irrecoverably remove insurance policy records.

The device only supports Wi-Fi protocols vulnerable to

A flaw was found in openstack-network-exporter. When an operator configures user authentication but omits or misconfigures Transport Layer Security (TLS), the basic authentication mechanism is silently bypassed. This fail-open design allows an adjacent network attacker to access sensitive Open vSwitch (OVS) and Open Virtual Network (OVN) dataplane metrics without credentials. Consequently, an attacker can enumerate bridge names, port counters, OVN controller state, and host topology, leading to information disclosure.

A flaw was found in openstack-network-exporter. The HTTP server within the component is configured without essential timeout settings, such as ReadHeaderTimeout. This vulnerability allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker to initiate multiple slow HTTP header connections. By trickling header bytes, the attacker can exhaust server resources, specifically file descriptors, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) that prevents legitimate Prometheus metric scraping and alerting.

SonicWall SMA1000 Appliances contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to gain unauthorized access to sensitive functionality and perform unauthorized operations.
Out-of-bounds read in Microsoft Bluetooth Driver allows an unauthorized attacker to elevate privileges with a physical attack.
Heap-based buffer overflow in Microsoft Internet Messaging API allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.

Improper neutralization of section delimiters in job files read by the Checkmk agents for Linux, AIX, Solaris, FreeBSD and OpenWrt in Checkmk <2.5.0p15, <2.4.0p38, <2.3.0p51 and 2.2.0 (EOL) allows a local user for whom mk-job job monitoring has been set up to inject arbitrary agent sections and piggyback data into the agent output, spoofing monitoring data of the monitored host and of other hosts, or hiding and impersonating the jobs of other users.

A flaw was found in the jwcrypto library, which is used for implementing Javascript Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) standards. The issue occurs when the library verifies a General JSON Serialization JWS using a set of keys. Due to a coding error, the library fails to correctly identify the specific key ID (kid) and may instead accept a signature made by any valid key in the set. This can allow an attacker with a valid key to bypass authorization checks in applications that rely on the key ID to identify specific tenants or users.

A flaw was found in rpm. A local attacker could supply a specially crafted `.gem` filename containing RPM macro syntax. When a user or automated workflow invokes `rpmuncompress -x` on this file, the macro expansion occurs during command construction. This allows the attacker to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the invoking account, leading to a compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

A flaw was found in the SFTP backend in gvfs. When mounting a share, a malicious SFTP server can cause read_string() to allocate a buffer with a certain length but the function does not verify that the buffer is completely filled, leaving the remainder of the buffer containing uninitialized heap contents. If the server sends a short FXP_HANDLE reply, these uninitialized bytes are taken as the file handle. The client will then echo these uninitialized bytes back to the server on all subsequent requests using that handle. With a length of 128 bytes, this issue allows the malicious server to deterministically read uninitialized heap memory from the gvfsd-sftp process, leaking its heap base and the load address of the libgio library, resulting in a deterministic defeat of Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR).

A flaw was found in the AFP backend in gvfs. When mounting a share, a malicious AFP server can cause the DSI read path to process a length that exceeds the size requested by the client. The function does not verify the server-provided length against the pre-sized reply buffer, causing the operation to access past the intended boundaries. This issue allows a malicious server to overflow a heap buffer and crash the gvfsd-afp process, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in the MTP backend in gvfs. When reading a file from a mounted MTP device, do_read() in gvfsbackendmtp.c trusts the data length returned by the device without limiting it to the original size requested by the client. If a malicious MTP device responds with more bytes than requested, this unrestricted length is passed directly to memcpy(). This causes the operation to read memory outside the intended boundaries. This allows an attacker who plugs in a malicious MTP device to cause a segmentation fault when a file is read and crash the gvfsd-mtp process, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in ansible-core's ansible.builtin.git module. The module
invokes git (ls-remote, clone, fetch) with the repository URL as a positional
argument and without a "--" separator, so a repository URL that begins with a
dash is interpreted by git as a command-line option. A caller that passes an
attacker-controlled repository URL to the module can trigger argument
injection (for example --upload-pack/--exec), resulting in arbitrary command
execution on the host running the module.
Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway contain an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer vulnerability which could lead to denial of service.

Issue summary: A QUIC peer that sends many small out-of-order STREAM fragments
while withholding the first byte of the stream may cause OpenSSL to buffer
a large number of reassembly nodes occupying much larger memory than
the actual data sent.

Impact summary: A remote peer can pin large amounts of memory on a server that
accepts incoming QUIC streams, potentially exhausting memory and causing
Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: QUIC receive flow control limits the highest byte offset a peer
may reach on a stream. It does not limit how many out-of-order fragments the
receiver buffers. OpenSSL allocates a reassembly node for each non-adjacent
STREAM fragment and never caps the count. A peer that opens a stream and sends
many one-byte fragments at increasing offsets, while withholding the first
byte, makes the receiver retain one node per fragment without delivering any
data.

Only applications that accept incoming streams are exposed. With the default
policy, which rejects peer-initiated streams, the stream is torn down before
state accumulates. Because the read side never advances past the missing
prefix, the flow control window never slides and the nodes stay pinned for the
life of the connection.

The per-stream window bounds the highest offset, so the memory one stream can
pin is finite, but it can reach tens of megabytes and, across many streams and
connections, drive memory pressure and Denial of Service. The severity is
limited because the exhaustion is bounded by flow control and requires a
non-default configuration.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL
pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA
records.

Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial
of Service).

CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference

Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at
least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2)
usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted
CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of
associated TLSA records.

DANE SMTP clients should not be affected since only the
DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) TLSA record usages are specified applicable
in SMTP.  For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim
MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.

Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also
unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.

Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI
are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses
OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.

FIPS impact: no
The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

A flaw was found in WildFly. A user with the `Monitor` role, which is the lowest standard Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) role, can exploit a path traversal vulnerability in the `take-snapshot` operation. By manipulating the `name` parameter, this user can write a copy of the server configuration to an arbitrary location. This allows the `Monitor` role to read back the server configuration, including sensitive credentials, which would otherwise be restricted by RBAC, leading to information disclosure.

A flaw was found in PCS (Pacemaker Configuration System). A local attacker with membership in the 'haclient' group can exploit the 'pcs host auth --token' command to read the contents of arbitrary files on the filesystem, provided the files are shorter than 256 bytes. The file contents are read with root privileges by the pcsd daemon and can be exfiltrated by the attacker through subsequent cluster node communication. This allows disclosure of sensitive data such as API keys, tokens, or configuration secrets that would otherwise be inaccessible to the attacker.

A flaw was found in rpm. An attacker can exploit a command injection vulnerability by influencing the path or filename of a tarball processed by `rpmbuild -t*` to include shell metacharacters. This is particularly relevant in automated build or continuous integration (CI) workflows that ingest externally supplied artifact names. Successful exploitation allows for arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the build user, which could lead to information disclosure or disruption of the build environment.

A flaw was found in rpmuncompress. This command injection vulnerability allows a local attacker to execute arbitrary commands. This occurs when rpmuncompress processes a specially crafted archive filename containing shell metacharacters, which are not properly escaped before being passed to shell command strings. Successful exploitation requires user interaction, where a user or automated workflow invokes rpmuncompress on the malicious file, leading to high impact on the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data accessible to the invoking user.

A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in GStreamer's RTSP support library. The vulnerability occurs while parsing an Authorization or WWW-Authenticate header that uses Digest authentication. Specially crafted whitespace placement around a parameter's terminator can cause an internal length calculation to underflow, leading to a crash of the process parsing the header. On an RTSP server this can be triggered by a remote, unauthenticated attacker sending a single malformed request when the server has authentication enabled; the same flaw can also be triggered against an RTSP client by a malicious or compromised RTSP server. Successful exploitation results in a denial of service (application crash) and has no confirmed impact on confidentiality or integrity.

A flaw was found in libtirpc. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending oversized wrapped data requests to an RPC (Remote Procedure Call) service configured with RPCSEC_GSS (Remote Procedure Call Security-Generic Security Service) integrity or privacy. This can lead to unbounded memory allocation, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting system resources and causing the service to become unstable or terminate.

A flaw was found in polkit. When processing input that begins with a null byte, an arithmetic error in the authentication agent helper causes an integer underflow during buffer length calculation, resulting in an out-of-bounds memory read. An attacker capable of supplying crafted input can trigger this flaw, potentially causing an application crash and resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in OpenSCAP. When decomposing a Source DataStream (SDS) file, the application does not properly validate relative file path attributes, leading to a path traversal vulnerability. An attacker can exploit this flaw by tricking a user or automated system into decomposing a crafted datastream containing directory traversal sequences. Successful exploitation allows unauthorized file creation or modification outside the intended target directory with the permissions of the executing process.

A flaw was found in libsoup. When a client sends an HTTP/2 request body from a non-pollable input stream, the library can buffer more data than the current flow-control window later allows. A malicious HTTP/2 server can shrink SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE while that buffered read is still in progress. The client then copies the full buffer into a smaller DATA callback without a runtime bounds check, which can abort the process or fail the HTTP/2 session.

A flaw was found in libtpms, a library that provides software TPM 2.0 emulation. When restoring TPM 2.0 state (for example during a virtual machine's power-on or state/migration restore), a malformed state blob can supply an oversized skip-block length that is not validated against the remaining size of the input buffer. This can drive an internal size counter negative, which bypasses a subsequent bounds check due to an unsafe signed-to-unsigned conversion, causing the parser to read memory outside the bounds of the heap buffer holding the state data. Successful exploitation can crash the process hosting libtpms (such as swtpm), resulting in a denial of service of the emulated TPM device and the virtual machine that depends on it. No data corruption or information disclosure was confirmed.
Buffer over-read in Servicing Stack Updates allows an authorized attacker to disclose information locally.

A flaw was found in libtirpc. A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted PMAPPROC_DUMP replies to a client application that uses the pmap_getmaps() function against an attacker-controlled host. This unbounded decoding can lead to excessive memory and CPU allocation, causing the client process to experience a Denial of Service (DoS) due to resource exhaustion.

Under some configurations a request to the ping endpoint could carry out more than a simple health check. In deployments that rely on Solr's rule-based authorization, a client granted only the low-privilege health permission could thereby trigger behavior that should require higher privileges; where the shipped security.json template leaves the health permission unauthenticated, no credentials are required at all. 


This issue affects Apache Solr from 9.0.0 through the releases preceding the fixed versions. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 9.11.0 or 10.1.0, which resolve the issue.




You are affected if you run an affected version and allow the /admin/ping endpoint to be reached with only the health permission. This includes the default sample security configuration installed by the bin/solr CLI, where that endpoint is unauthenticated.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should restrict access to the /admin/ping endpoint in their authorization configuration — for example by requiring a trusted role for that path — and ensure Solr is not reachable from untrusted clients or networks, as recommended for all Solr deployments.

A missing authorization check has been found in the user_mail_notifications function in mail_notifications_controller.rb of the mail notification API in the foreman package. The action returns another user's notification settings when only the generic view permission for mail notifications is present. A low-privileged network attacker or user who can view mail notifications can request any user id and read that user's subscription choices and stored mail search strings.

A missing authorization check has been found in the find_user function in user_aware.rb of the SSH key API in the foreman package. The create action attaches a new public key to the user id in the request without checking that the caller may edit that user. A low-privileged network attacker or user who already holds permission to create SSH keys can add their key to another user's account. That key is then stored with the victim and can be used by features that export that user's SSH keys.

A flaw was found in 389-ds-base. The server does not discard plaintext bytes already buffered from a client connection when negotiating StartTLS, allowing an on-path attacker to inject a crafted LDAP message that is processed after the TLS upgrade and whose response is delivered to the client in place of the client's own pending operation's response, due to messageID collision. This can cause a client application to treat a failed authentication (bind) attempt as successful.

A flaw was found in GLib2. When g_file_replace() is used with G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION and creating the .goutputstream-XXXXXX temporary file fails, the library unlinks the destination and recreates it without exclusive creation or symlink protection. A local attacker who can write to the destination directory can win that race and redirect the write to another file.

A flaw was found in gst-plugins-base. A heap buffer overflow can be triggered when processing video buffers whose attached GstVideoMeta metadata declares plane strides and offsets that exceed the actual backing memory allocation. The metadata is not range-checked during deserialization, and the video frame mapping code does not verify that the declared plane geometry fits within the buffer before allowing consumers to read or write video data. A local attacker who controls the sending side of a GStreamer inter-process IPC pipeline can deliver a crafted buffer carrying fabricated strides, causing the receiving process to read or write beyond heap boundaries. Successful exploitation can cause a denial of service or potentially allow code execution within the affected process.
A flaw was found in DPDK lib/vhost. Missing length validation before reading command_data in the virtio-net control-queue handler can cause an out-of-bounds read and a host process crash.

A remote attacker may be able to terminate a process that passes attacker-controlled input to the P-384 VOPRF API without bounding its length. This vulnerability is addressed in swift-crypto version 5.0.3.
An authorization issue was addressed with improved entitlement checks. This issue is fixed in iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2. A remote attacker may be able to access sensitive user data.

Crypt::JWT versions before 0.037_1 for Perl compare HMAC signatures and JWE authentication tags in non-constant time.

decode_jwt compares HS256, HS384 and HS512 signatures, and the authentication tag of A128CBC-HS256, A192CBC-HS384 and A256CBC-HS512 encrypted tokens, against the computed value with Perl's eq operator. Its run time depends on the number of matching leading bytes.

An attacker who can submit many candidate tokens and measure the timing precisely enough may recover the expected signature or tag byte by byte and forge a token that verifies.

Authorization bypass through User-Controlled key vulnerability in İdeal Data Finansal Teknolojiler A.Ş. IDeal WEB allows Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs.

A flaw was found in SSSD's IdP authentication provider. The eval_access_token_buf() function compares the OIDC subject identifier using strncmp() with the authenticated user's identifier length, performing a prefix comparison instead of an exact match. An attacker whose IdP identifier is a strict prefix of a target user's identifier can authenticate as the target user.

The cupsUTF32ToUTF8() function in CUPS's cups/transcode.c lacks a source-length bound and can read past the end of the source buffer, resulting in a heap out-of-bounds read. This is reachable via SNMP supply-description parsing in backend/snmp-supplies.c with attacker-controlled content.

Two case-insensitive comparisons on request-derived usernames outside the main authorization path in CUPS's scheduler (printer ACL validation and private-attribute filtering) could allow bypass of username-based access controls in certain configurations.

Improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic in the GridFS component of the MongoDB Go Driver can cause a caller-supplied structured file identifier to be interpreted as a query condition rather than as a literal identifier. An authenticated user who can influence the identifier passed by an affected application may cause all GridFS file chunks in the affected bucket to be removed, rendering stored file content unreadable.
Missing authorization in Microsoft Office SharePoint allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

A flaw was found in sssd. A local user can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting the responder service's available file descriptors (system handles used for open connections). By opening and maintaining many concurrent connections to a responder socket while continuing to queue new connection attempts, an attacker can trigger an unthrottled retry loop. This condition leads to high CPU utilization and stalls the service, preventing legitimate identity and authentication requests from being processed.

A flaw was found in crun. When the container configuration does not give /dev a dedicated mount, terminal setup can redirect /dev/console onto an attacker-controlled path, including via the read-only-rootfs bind-mount fallback. Affected versions are crun 1.29.1 and earlier. Default configurations that mount a fresh /dev are not exposed. No fixed release is available yet.

A flaw was found in crun. After pivot_root, reopening /dev/null for stdio can follow a symlink and attach a host file to container stdio, then change that file's ownership. Affected versions are crun 1.29.1 and earlier. Default configurations that mount a fresh /dev are not exposed. No fixed release is available yet.

Improper neutralization of special elements used in an OS command in certain ASUS Router firmware models allows an remote attacker to to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges by inducing a logged-in administrator to visit a malicious website.
Refer to the ' Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

Missing Authentication for Critical
Function in certain ASUS Router firmware allows unauthenticated nearby users to
obtain router information and resources (e.g., multimedia files) via HTTP
requests.
Refer to the ' Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

The Web-Based Management (WBM) authorization model does not properly enforce permissions for all PROFIBUS configuration operations. A low-privileged remote attacker can abuse an exposed configuration function to modify root-owned PROFIBUS parameters, including device addressing and SSA settings. This allows unauthorized changes to fieldbus-related configuration and violates the intended privilege boundaries within the management interface.

A flaw was found in Evolution. A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted HTML email containing a spoofed vCard control. When a victim clicks on this control, Evolution's trusted JavaScript handler incorrectly assigns an attacker-controlled JavaScript URL to an iframe's source. This action leads to arbitrary JavaScript execution within the mail-viewing context, effectively bypassing the security measures designed to prevent script execution in email content.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-good isomp4 plugin. When processing a specially crafted MP4 or MOV file containing CEA-608 closed-caption data, an integer overflow in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic can bypass a bounds check in the caption parser. This leads to an out-of-bounds heap read of up to 244 bytes, which is then included in the downstream caption output. An attacker could exploit this by tricking a user into opening a malicious media file, potentially resulting in disclosure of adjacent heap memory or application crash.

A flaw was found in RESTEasy's CorsFilter, which, when configured to allow all origins ("*"), reflects the request's Origin header back in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This permissive cross-origin policy allows a malicious website to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read authenticated responses from a victim's session, resulting in a loss of confidentiality.

A flaw was found in RESTEasy's IIOImageProvider, which decodes attacker-supplied image request bodies without enforcing any limit on the declared image dimensions or pixel count. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a small crafted image declaring enormous dimensions to trigger a very large memory allocation, exhausting the JVM heap and resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in parted. A heap-based buffer overflow can occur when processing a specially crafted FAT32 filesystem due to an integer calculation error during buffer allocation. A local attacker could exploit this by enticing a user or automated service to open a malicious filesystem image, resulting in an application crash leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) or potential memory corruption.

A flaw was found in parted. A heap-based buffer overflow exists in libparted's file system resizing logic when handling FAT16 volumes. By convincing a user or administrator to resize a specially crafted FAT16 file system image with malformed directory metadata, an attacker can trigger an oversized read into a fixed-size memory buffer. This issue causes memory corruption, resulting in an application crash and a denial of service (DoS).

A flaw was found in nfs-utils. An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending repeated state notification requests to an exposed rpc.statd service. The service fails to properly release memory allocated during callback processing, leading to continuous memory growth. Sustained requests can exhaust system resources, eventually causing the service to degrade or crash.

A flaw was found in nfs-utils. The fsidd daemon improperly handles input received over its local domain socket by relying on program assertions to verify command arguments. A local user can exploit this vulnerability by sending a malformed request lacking the required arguments to trigger an assertion failure. This causes the daemon to crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) for filesystem identifier lookup services until restarted.

A flaw was found in `multipathd`. A local attacker with access to the `multipathd` UNIX control socket can exploit this vulnerability by sending valid commands and then ceasing to read replies. This action can cause the `multipathd` listener thread to block, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) where legitimate Inter-Process Communication (IPC) operations may hang or time out. This issue does not result in privilege escalation, arbitrary code execution, or impact data confidentiality or integrity.

A flaw was found in SSSD. When configured with the LDAP access provider and `ldap_access_order` including `ppolicy` or `lockout`, a fail-open condition in the LDAP ppolicy access check can occur if a user lookup returns zero results. This can incorrectly return success and cache an allow decision, permitting continued authorization for a deleted or deprovisioned user. A remote attacker with prior valid account context could exploit this to maintain access to information and potentially make limited modifications to resources that should no longer be available.

A flaw was found in the sssd NSS responder. This input validation vulnerability allows a local attacker, by sending specially crafted service lookup requests to the NSS responder's UNIX socket, to cause an out-of-bounds read. This out-of-bounds read may lead to a denial of service (DoS) by crashing the NSS responder process. While unprivileged local clients can typically reach the socket, there is no evidence of privilege escalation or reliable data disclosure.

The ITE it51xxx I2C driver, when operating as an I2C target (slave) in buffer mode (CONFIG_I2C_TARGET + CONFIG_I2C_TARGET_BUFFER_MODE), transmits response data from the fixed-size data->target_out_buffer inside its target FIFO interrupt handler target_i2c_isr_fifo() in drivers/i2c/i2c_ite_it51xxx.c. On every data interrupt of a host read transaction the handler pushes a fixed 16 bytes from target_out_buffer[i + data->r_index] into the hardware FIFO and then advances data->r_index by 16, without ever checking that index against the size of the buffer.

data->r_index is reset to zero only on a STOP or timeout condition, so within a single transaction it only accumulates. An I2C host that keeps clocking read bytes without issuing STOP drives data->r_index past the end of the buffer after sixteen interrupts (default CONFIG_I2C_TARGET_IT51XXX_MAX_BUF_SIZE = 256 bytes), and every interrupt after that reads 16 bytes from beyond target_out_buffer and places them on the bus. What follows the buffer in the driver's device data structure is data->target_shared_fifo and the remaining static device state, so a sufficiently long read transaction streams adjacent firmware memory to the host.

The same handler, and the shared-FIFO arm of target_i2c_isr_pio(), also declare the transfer length uninitialised and invoke the optional buf_read_requested() callback without checking that it is registered. A target that supplies no read callback leaves the source pointer NULL and the length indeterminate; when that length compares below the destination size, memcpy() runs with a NULL source. Because the transmit path feeds the FIFO whether or not the callback provided data, such a target also places whatever the previous request left in the buffer onto the bus.

The trigger is a malicious or misbehaving I2C master on the same bus (for example a compromised application processor or a rogue device on an exposed I2C bus); no software privilege on the victim is required and the handler runs in the target's kernel/firmware context. The disclosed bytes are not attacker-chosen, but their extent is: the host controls how long the transaction runs and therefore how far past the buffer the driver reads.

This is the read-direction counterpart of CVE-2026-14986, which closed the write direction of the same routine without adding the matching bound on the read path.

A flaw was found in foreman-mcp-server. This component utilizes two distinct logging mechanisms that can expose sensitive session and authentication data. One mechanism logs session identifiers, which are treated as authentication credentials, at an informational level. The other, when debug logging is enabled, incompletely sanitizes HTTP request headers, leading to the cleartext logging of sensitive information such as authorization tokens and API keys. This vulnerability can result in a confidentiality breach, as sensitive authentication data is persisted in plain text within container logs, increasing the risk if logs are forwarded to a centralized platform.

A flaw was found in sssd, specifically within the PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) responder's protocol v1 parser, pam_parse_in_data(). A local client with access to the PAM responder's UNIX socket can exploit this by negotiating protocol v1 and sending an empty or truncated PAM request body. This can trigger an out-of-bounds read, potentially causing the PAM responder to terminate or restart, leading to a local denial of service.

A flaw was found in SSSD (System Security Services Daemon). A local attacker with privileges to connect to the PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) responder socket can send a specially crafted protocol request. If the `pam_app_services` configuration is enabled and the service item is omitted from the request, a NULL pointer dereference can occur. This vulnerability leads to a denial of service, causing the PAM responder to crash and disrupt authentication services.

A flaw was found in sssd. A local unprivileged user could send a specially crafted request with a zero-length body to the Network Security Services (NSS) responder. This could lead to a denial-of-service condition, causing the NSS responder to become unstable or terminate. This vulnerability affects the availability of the system responder.

A flaw was found in Cockpit. An authenticated local user with a large user identifier (UID) can cause unauthorized modification and disclosure of login records. On 32-bit systems, an integer overflow during session accounting allows the user's login process to read or overwrite the legacy log entries of other accounts.

A flaw was found in Cockpit. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by initiating and sustaining numerous simultaneous connections to the `cockpit-tls` service. This forces the service to create an unbounded number of detached threads, consuming system resources such as memory and file descriptors. The primary consequence is a denial of service (DoS), leading to degradation or complete unavailability of the Cockpit service for legitimate users.

A flaw was found in cockpit-files. This vulnerability allows a local attacker to exploit a timing issue, known as a symlink race condition, during privileged file operations such as changing file ownership or permissions. By manipulating directory entries and winning this race, the attacker can redirect these operations to unintended files. This could lead to unauthorized changes in file ownership and permissions on arbitrary files, potentially compromising system integrity and availability by altering system or application states or rendering services unusable.

A flaw was found in libsolv. This heap buffer overflow vulnerability occurs when a victim processes a specially crafted `.solv` file containing negative size values in the `repo_add_solv` function. This leads to an undersized memory allocation and a subsequent out-of-bounds write. An attacker could exploit this to cause a denial of service (DoS).

A flaw was found in libsolv. This stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability occurs in libsolv's Debian metadata parser when processing specially crafted Debian repository metadata. An attacker could exploit this by providing malicious SHA384 or SHA512 checksum tags, leading to memory corruption and a denial of service (DoS) in the affected system.

LimeSurvey 7.0.14 fails to encode attacker-controlled values from a crafted LSS survey file when displaying import warnings. An attacker can persuade an authenticated user with surveys:create permission to import the file, causing JavaScript to execute in that user's LimeSurvey session.

A flaw was found in GNOME Shell. When processing icons from a remote search provider via D-Bus, the system fails to validate the icon's declared dimensions against the actual data buffer size. A malicious or compromised remote search provider could exploit this by providing oversized icon dimensions, leading to an out-of-bounds read. This can cause the GNOME Shell process to crash, disrupting the user's session, and potentially disclose sensitive information from adjacent memory.

A flaw was found in the ChunkReader component of the Undertow web server, which is used to handle chunked transfer encoding in HTTP requests. The issue occurs because a security check for the chunk size is performed before the value is shifted, allowing a specifically crafted 15-digit chunk size to bypass the limit and overflow into internal state flags. This can cause the server to terminate a request body prematurely and interpret the remaining data as a separate, smuggled request.

A flaw was found in gss-ntlmssp. A memory leak occurs in the NTLM target-info parser when a crafted NTLM CHALLENGE message contains duplicated string-valued AV_PAIR entries. The parser allocates memory for each string value but does not free the previous allocation when the same AV_PAIR type appears more than once, leaking the earlier allocation. A malicious or man-in-the-middle server can exploit this to cause gradual memory exhaustion on the client during NTLM authentication, leading to a denial of service.

Missing authorization in the REST API endpoint for updating the discovery phase of a single service in Checkmk <2.5.0p14, <2.4.0p37, <2.3.0p51 and 2.2.0 (EOL) allows an authenticated user whose role holds the four "Service discovery" permissions but lacks "Make changes, perform actions" or "Manage services" to move, disable or remove services on hosts the user can read.

A flaw was found in jwcrypto. The JWK.import_key() function validates the key_ops JWK member for duplicate values using an algorithm with O(n^2) time complexity, and the length of key_ops is not bounded. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can supply a JWK with a large key_ops array to an application that passes attacker-controlled key material to a public key-import API (reachable via ECDH-ES key agreement, OIDC dynamic client registration, DPoP, or ACME account key registration, among others) to consume excessive CPU time, resulting in a denial of service.
Rejected reason: not a vulnerability

An out-of-bounds write flaw was found in usbredir. Starting an isochronous OUT stream with a transfer count of 1 leaves the stream's single transfer buffer permanently unsubmitted, defeating the bounds check in usbredirhost_iso_packet() and allowing a usbredir peer to write past the end of the packet descriptor array on every subsequent isochronous packet.

LimeSurvey 7.0.14 contains a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in the survey-participant CSV import result page. An attacker can supply a CSV with a crafted invalid attribute column name and persuade an authenticated user with tokens:import permission to import it with Display attribute warnings enabled. The import result echoes the header value without HTML encoding, executing script in the victim's LimeSurvey session.

HashiCorp Vault and Vault Enterprise are vulnerable to an issue in the integrated storage join process that may allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a new, uninitialized node to cause that node to send credentials from its server environment to an attacker-controlled server. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-92735) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.25.

Vault's Login MFA feature did not consistently enforce the lifetime of pending two-phase login requests. This may allow a user who previously completed the first authentication factor to complete MFA and obtain a Vault token after the pending request should have expired, including after the user's primary credential has been rotated. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-92738) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.26.

A flaw was found in SSSD. When configured to evaluate password expiration warnings before restrictive access rules in LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) environments, an expired-password warning terminates rule evaluation early and treats the access request as successful. A remote authenticated user with an expired password using an alternative authentication method, such as SSH public key authentication, can exploit this flaw to bypass access control restrictions and gain unauthorized access to protected systems.

A flaw was found in libmodulemd. When parsing module metadata, the xmd field is converted into nested GVariant values through recursive YAML mapping and sequence helpers without a recursion-depth or node-count limit. An attacker who can supply crafted modulemd YAML with deeply nested xmd content can cause stack exhaustion or excessive resource consumption, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in libmodulemd. In builds with rpmio support enabled, compressed modulemd YAML is decompressed through a custom read handler that does not enforce a cumulative decompressed-size limit before parsing. An attacker who can supply a highly compressible compressed YAML file can cause excessive CPU and memory consumption, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in libmodulemd. In the module stream v2 rpm-map emission path, an inner loop incorrectly uses the count of digest algorithms as its bound instead of the number of checksums in the current digest table. Crafted modulemd v2 metadata with multiple digest types can trigger an out-of-bounds read during YAML serialization, typically causing a crash and resulting in a denial of service.
IBM watsonx.data 2.4.0 through 2.4.0 patch 8 could allow a remote authenticated attacker to conduct a server-side request forgery due to a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability.

A flaw was found in Redis community. The cluster bus packet parser, responsible for handling PING, PONG, and MEET packets, fails to properly validate string-carrying extensions for null-termination. This oversight allows a remote attacker to craft a malicious packet, leading to an out-of-bounds read when the packet's payload is processed. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could result in the disclosure of sensitive information or a remote denial of service (DoS).

A flaw was found in dnsmasq. The TFTP server can serve the wrong file contents because a recently used transfer cache is not invalidated when a transfer finishes. An attacker on the local network who can request a TFTP file may cause a later client to receive previously cached data instead of the requested file. In PXE network-boot environments this can substitute attacker-chosen boot content for a victim machine.

A flaw was found in dnsmasq. The TCP DNS service uses a small fixed pool of child processes and does not set a receive timeout on client connections. A remote attacker can open idle TCP connections to port 53 and occupy the entire pool, preventing new TCP DNS connections and DNSSEC validation that requires TCP fallback. UDP DNS resolution continues, and occupied slots are released after a fixed lifetime.

A flaw was found in dnsmasq. The DHCPv6 client hostname parser can read one byte past the end of a crafted FQDN option because it checks the next label length before confirming the pointer is still inside the option. An attacker on the local network can trigger this with a single DHCPv6 packet. The extra byte is not returned to the client or logged, and no crash has been demonstrated.

A flaw was found in dnsmasq. When DHCP leasequery is enabled without listing allowed source addresses, the server does not check who sent the query. A host on the local network can request DHCP lease records and learn assigned addresses, MAC addresses, hostnames, and related lease metadata. The feature is off unless an administrator turns it on.

A flaw was found in dnsmasq. After a reduction of internal domain-name buffer sizes, the DNSSEC validator can write a few bytes past a name buffer when converting names to and from DNS wire format. An attacker who can cause the server to validate a crafted DNSSEC response may overwrite a small amount of adjacent heap metadata. DNSSEC support is not compiled in by default and must also be enabled at runtime.

Vault's audit devices did not validate the contents of a configured audit log prefix and did not consistently enforce the server-level setting that restricts audit log prefixing. This may allow a privileged operator to inject content into audit logs, potentially leading to forged or misleading audit records. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-93333) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.25.

Vault Community Edition and Vault Enterprise did not consistently apply explicit ACL policy deny rules to request paths that differ only by a trailing slash. This may allow an authenticated user who holds a broader delete permission on system configuration paths to disable a secrets engine, auth method, or audit device that a more specific deny rule was intended to protect. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-93335) is fixed in Vault Community Edition 2.2.2 and Vault Enterprise 2.2.2, 1.21.14, and 1.19.25.

A flaw was found in libstoragemgmt. An attacker with control over a local or virtual storage device could provide specially crafted SCSI (Small Computer System Interface) Vital Product Data (VPD) page 0x80 data. This malformed data, specifically an untrusted page length field, can lead to a stack buffer overflow in the `_sg_parse_vpd_80()` function during serial number parsing. Successful exploitation could result in a denial of service by crashing or destabilizing the process querying the serial number.

Out-of-bounds write vulnerability in certain ASUS routers allows an unauthenticated nearby user to corrupt process memory, potentially resulting in a denial-of-service, via crafted LLTD packets.Refer to the ' Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

Insertion of sensitive information into sent data in certain ASUS Router firmware allows a remote attacker to obtain router’s UID or login authorization tokens for the victim's linked account via a crafted web page, which requires a logged-in router administrator to actively complete the third-party authorization flow.
Refer to the '
Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

Use of externally-controlled format string in certain ASUS Router firmware allows a nearby administrator to read or write memory, potentially resulting in a denial-of-service, via crafted format specifiers sent to the logging/summary function.
Refer to the ' Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

A flaw was found in Netty. SpdySessionHandler accepts an unlimited number of concurrent remote-initiated streams because localConcurrentStreams defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE and the handler provides no API to change it. A remote peer can open a SPDY connection and send a large number of SYN_STREAM frames with FLAG_FIN=0, causing unbounded heap and direct memory allocation that can lead to JVM OutOfMemoryError and a denial of service.

A flaw was found in Netty's HttpServerCodec. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability by pipelining HTTP/1.1 requests on a single connection and withholding reads. This action causes the methodOverflowQueue to grow without limit, leading to unbounded heap memory consumption and a denial of service due to memory exhaustion.

A flaw was found in Netty's HTTP/2 HpackEncoder. A remote attacker can exploit this by sending HTTP/2 SETTINGS frames with a very large MAX_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE. This causes the HpackEncoder to store an excessive number of unique headers, leading to increased CPU usage and memory consumption, ultimately resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in Netty's WebSocketServerExtensionHandler. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability by using HTTP/1.1 pipelining to send requests faster than the application can respond. This leads to an unbounded growth of a per-connection queue, consuming excessive memory. Eventually, this can cause the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) to exhaust its heap, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) for the affected server.

A flaw was found in Netty's HTTP/1 decoder. Incomplete validation of malformed Transfer-Encoding headers allows a remote attacker to perform HTTP request smuggling. By sending specially crafted HTTP requests, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTTP requests, potentially bypassing security controls or accessing unauthorized resources.

A flaw was found in Netty. A reference-count leak in the HAProxy PROXY-v2 message decoder allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to send specially crafted PROXY-protocol v2 headers. This can lead to memory exhaustion, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) for the affected system.

A flaw was found in Netty RtspDecoder. The `RtspMethods.valueOf()` function incorrectly strips trailing control bytes from method tokens in Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) requests. A remote attacker can exploit this by sending a specially crafted RTSP request, leading to method-token smuggling. This vulnerability allows an attacker to bypass method-based access controls and can also be used to launder malicious requests through Netty-based RTSP proxies, making them appear legitimate to backend systems.

A flaw was found in Netty. A remote attacker could exploit this by sending a specially crafted HTTP request that includes control characters within the chunk-size line. This bypasses the intended strict validation, allowing the attacker to inject arbitrary HTTP requests. This vulnerability can lead to HTTP request smuggling, potentially resulting in information disclosure or other unauthorized actions.

A flaw was found in Netty's HTTP/2 codec. When converting HTTP/1 CONNECT requests to HTTP/2, the component incorrectly uses the Host header instead of the CONNECT authority-form request-target for the tunnel authority. A remote attacker can exploit this by supplying a different Host header, leading to a malformed HTTP/2 CONNECT request. This can bypass security controls such as tunnel allow-lists or egress policies, resulting in integrity loss.

A flaw was found in Netty. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 Extended CONNECT requests. Netty's HTTP-object conversion path incorrectly processes these requests as regular HTTP/1.1 CONNECT requests, leading to a loss of critical protocol and path information. This misinterpretation can allow attackers to bypass security policies, such as routing or authorization logic, in applications that rely on Netty for HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 communication, resulting in integrity loss.

A flaw was found in Netty. A remote unauthenticated attacker can exploit a vulnerability in Netty's HTTP/1 to HTTP/2 conversion process. When an HTTP/1 request includes both an absolute-form request-target and a conflicting Host header, Netty incorrectly prioritizes the Host header for the HTTP/2 :authority field, discarding the original request-target authority. This inconsistency can allow an attacker to bypass security controls in Netty-based proxies or gateways, potentially leading to unauthorized access, cache poisoning, or misrouting of requests.

A flaw was found in Netty's HTTP/1.1 decoder. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to bypass `Transfer-Encoding` header validation by splitting the `Transfer-Encoding` field across multiple headers, with the last field containing a non-final transfer coding like `gzip` or `deflate`. This bypass can lead to HTTP request smuggling, enabling attackers to bypass security controls, desynchronize request processing, or cause requests to be processed in an unintended context.

A flaw was found in Netty's `netty-codec-http` component. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted HTTP/1.1 chunk-size token that includes post-digit whitespace. This incorrect parsing of the chunk size can lead to HTTP request smuggling. This allows an attacker to bypass security controls or access unauthorized resources in proxy/backend deployments.

A flaw was found in Netty's HTTP/2 stack. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to inject prohibited characters, such as NUL, Line Feed, and Carriage Return, into HTTP/2 header field values due to insufficient validation. When these values cross an HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 translation boundary, they can be exploited for request smuggling, header injection, or response splitting. This could lead to unauthorized access, data manipulation, or other security bypasses.

An SQL injection vulnerability in OTRS versions 2024.3.1 through 2026.8.1 allows unauthenticated remote attackers to inject arbitrary SQL expressions through the Survey endpoint.

The vulnerability exists in the Kernel::System::Survey::Request::RequestGet() method, which directly incorporates an attacker-controlled survey key into a SQL query without using parameterized statements. Successful exploitation allows attackers to retrieve ticket information and perform boolean-based or time-based blind SQL injection to extract potentially sensitive data accessible to the OTRS database account. Exploitation does not require authentication, a valid survey key, or an existing survey request. The external frontend must be accessible.

An improper authorization vulnerability in the EasyVistas EV Reach Client Agent allows authenticated users with low privileges to execute arbitrary commands on a remote Windows endpoint with LocalSystem privileges. The affected agent service does not sufficiently enforce authorization restrictions for certain privileged remote management operations. Under specific conditions, the agent fails to apply the intended user impersonation mechanism and executes user-supplied commands within the security context of the agent service, which runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

As a result, an authenticated attacker may bypass the intended privilege restrictions and execute arbitrary commands with the highest user-mode privileges on an affected Windows system. Successful exploitation may lead to complete compromise of the affected endpoint, including unauthorized access to sensitive information, modification of system configurations, installation of malicious software, or disruption of system availability. 

The vulnerability does not require administrative credentials or user interaction after successful authentication.

A denial of service flaw was found in Poppler's Splash backend. A crafted PDF with tiling-pattern geometry approaching the int32 boundary can cause SplashOutputDev::tilingPatternFill to compute an attacker-controlled repeat count that drives an excessively long loop in the pattern-fill scanline routine, without a corresponding memory allocation. An attacker could exploit this by supplying a malicious PDF to an application that renders it via Poppler's Splash backend, causing the rendering process to consume 100% CPU for an attacker-controlled, extended duration.

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability affecting Station Launcher App in 3DEXPERIENCE platform from Release 3DEXPERIENCE R2023x through Release 3DEXPERIENCE R2026x could lead to an unauthenticated remote code execution.
An authenticated WHMCS client could potentially leverage this flaw to read sensitive configuration files on the WHMCS host, including database credentials, and to execute code on the server.

HumHub 1.18.5 is affected by a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability that allows any user holding the delegated, non-system-administrator Manage Users permission (admin_manage_users) to inject persistent HTML/JavaScript into a Profile Field Category title.

An unauthenticated stored and reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the embedded web interface of Frontier Smart Technologies Venice X FS2340 running IR4.9 allows a network attacker with access to the interface to inject attacker-controlled JavaScript that may execute in the browser of a user accessing affected content.



Successful exploitation may allow the attacker to access information available within the browser's security context or perform actions through the affected web interface with the privileges of the affected user.



During authorized security testing, certain crafted JavaScript and code-injection payloads were also observed to cause the embedded web interface to crash and become temporarily unavailable on some tested software versions. This behavior represents a denial-of-service condition affecting the embedded web management interface; no device-level denial of service was established.

Improper neutralization of input during web page generation ('cross-site scripting') vulnerability in ITG Bilgisayar Teknolojileri Grubu Ltd. Şti. VSRM allows XSS Through HTTP Headers.

This issue affects vSRM: from v14.08.1 before v14.08.5.
Rejected reason: reserved but not needed
Heap-based buffer overflow in Windows GDI allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.
Heap-based buffer overflow in Windows Broadcast DVR User Service allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.
Stack-based buffer overflow in Windows COM allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. In 4.6.00, an unauthenticated attacker can place the configured domain in X-Forwarded-Host while choosing a different destination in the ordinary Host header. The earlier fix validates only the forwarded value in includes/mainfile.php, while set_ini_file() in includes/ini.php constructs an outbound cURL request from the separately retained NV_SERVER_NAME before the ordinary host is rejected. Redirect following can carry the blind request to an attacker-selected private host, port, and path and invoke internal HTTP endpoints. This issue is fixed in version 4.6.01.

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. From 4.5.00 until 4.6.01, an authenticated settings-module administrator can upload a PKCS#12 S/MIME certificate whose X.509 Subject CN contains path separators and traversal components. The smimeadd handler in admin/settings/smtp.php applies only an at-sign replacement before using the CN in .key, .crt, and .pem paths beneath data/certs. Traversal can select attacker-chosen paths outside data/certs, but writes remain constrained to already-existing writable directories and the permitted extensions. Within that constraint, attacker-controlled PEM data can overwrite certificate assets, including a DKIM private key; when the curl.cainfo PHP directive is empty, the attacker can also replace cacert.pem and undermine outbound TLS verification. This issue is fixed in version 4.6.01.

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. Prior to 4.5.12 and 4.6.02, an attacker who can reach an image-upload flow can upload a valid image with appended PHP short-tag code and a double-extension filename. NukeViet\Files\Upload::save_file() relied on verify_image(), which missed the <? short-open tag, while filename handling preserved embedded dots, validation inspected only the final extension, and an .htaccess rule blocked PHP extensions only at the end of the URI. On Apache mod_php systems configured with short_open_tag and a PHP extension handler, the stored polyglot can execute as PHP and run operating-system commands as the web-server user; PHP-FPM, nginx, and end-anchored handler configurations are not exposed to the execution step. This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.12 and 4.6.02.

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. From 4.5.00 until 4.5.13 and 4.6.02, an unauthenticated attacker can place a multiply encoded value in the news module search q parameter. $nv_Request->get_title() decodes and sanitizes the input once, but modules/news/funcs/search.php subsequently applies urldecode() after sanitization. The resulting raw keyword reaches the {KEY} search-input attribute through search_theme() and the no-results element through search_result_theme() in the default and mobile themes, permitting attribute or tag injection and same-origin JavaScript execution when a victim opens the crafted search URL. This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.13 and 4.6.02.

In PeriodicAdvertisingSynchronizer::OnPeriodicAdvertisingReport of periodic_advertising_synchronizer.cc, there is a possible resource exhaustion due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In BrEdrDynamicChannel of bredr_dynamic_channel.cc, there is a possible resource leak due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In OpalCommunicationManagerService of opal_communication_manager_service.cc, there is a possible use after free due to a race condition. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with User execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In CameraManagerBroker::~CameraManagerBroker of camera_manager_broker.cc, there is a possible use after free due to a race condition. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with User execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation.

In HttpFileRequestHandler::GetFilePath of http_file_request_handler.cc, there is a possible path traversal due to improper input validation. This could lead to remote information disclosure with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In RemoteCharacteristic of remote_characteristic.cc, there is a possible process abort due to a missing check that the object still exists when a queued read response is handled. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In OnPairingFailed of security_manager.cc, there is a possible crash due to a logic error in clearing the link encryption key after a failed pairing. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In ResolvePendingNotifyRequests of remote_characteristic.cc, there is a possible use after free due to a status callback that can destroy the object while its pending request queue is still being iterated. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In LogicalLink::SignalError of logical_link.cc, there is a possible use after free due to the object being destroyed by a callback while it is still iterating over its channels. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In OnPairingRequest of security_manager.cc, there is a possible process abort due to a missing check of the local IO capability when Secure Connections Only mode raises the required security level. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In OnEncryptionChange of security_manager.cc, there is a possible way to establish a bond marked as authenticated without completing authenticated pairing due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in the DHCPv6 and TFTP response builders of libslirp. When the host is configured with a small interface MTU, a guest-supplied DHCPv6 CLIENTID option or TFTP blksize option can overflow the reply buffer with attacker-controlled content and length, resulting in denial of service and potentially arbitrary code execution in the host process. The default interface MTU is not affected.

A flaw was found in FreeType, specifically within its CID font loader. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by tricking a user into opening content that embeds or references a specially crafted CID-keyed font. This crafted font can cause repeated allocations and decryptions of subroutine data across multiple font dictionaries, leading to excessive memory and CPU consumption. This can result in a denial of service (DoS) for the application or service processing the font, potentially causing it to hang or terminate.

A flaw was found in rpm. An attacker can supply a crafted manifest file that, when processed by a user or automation using `rpm -q -p` or similar manifest-processing flows, leads to arbitrary code execution. This occurs because manifest entries are unexpectedly macro-expanded before being opened, allowing embedded shell commands to run with the privileges of the `rpm` process. Successful exploitation can lead to a full compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability for the affected account.

A heap-based buffer overflow flaw was found in rpm. Parsing a symlink entry in an untrusted RPM package whose declared RPMTAG_LONGFILESIZES value is 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF causes an integer overflow in iterReadArchiveNext() that shrinks a buffer allocation to one byte, after which the payload's independently-controlled cpio filesize field is used to write attacker-controlled data past the end of that allocation. This is reachable via rpm2cpio, rpm2archive, and rpm -qlvp on an  untrusted package.

A command injection flaw was found in rpm. Installing or rebuilding a source RPM whose source or spec file basenames contain a %() macro construct causes rpm to execute an attacker-controlled shell command via popen() while relocating the source file list. This allows arbitrary command execution as the invoking (typically non-root) user, simply by installing, rebuilding, or otherwise processing an untrusted .src.rpm.

An API which can allow a user to delete any workflow execution results is missing authentication. This means that any workflow result could be deleted by someone able to reach the Texera instance.



This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue.

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the computing unit workflow websocket of Apache Texera (incubating) allows an authenticated user to view workflow results, control workflow executions, and run code in a computing unit they have not been granted. In local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments this is possible directly; in Kubernetes deployments it is possible from code running inside another computing unit in the cluster.



This issue affects Apache Texera : from 1.1.0 through 1.2.0.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0, which fixes the issue. Local JVM and Docker Compose deployments do not provide the full security model and should only be used by trusted users.

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the project REST API of Apache Texera (incubating).



The project API did not check that the caller owns, or has been granted access to, the project being accessed. Any authenticated user with an approved account (the REGULAR or ADMIN role; new accounts need administrator approval by default) could view, modify or delete other users' projects, change which workflows those projects contain, and see the e-mail addresses of a project's owner and collaborators. The project feature is hidden in the web UI by default, but the API was reachable regardless of that setting.



This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue by removing the deprecated project feature and its data.



If you cannot upgrade immediately, configure the reverse proxy in front of Texera to reject every request whose path starts with /api/project, /api/public/project or /api/access/project, and every request whose path contains ';', which the Texera server ignores when routing. Respond with 403 or 404, not 401: from 1.2.0-incubating the web UI treats a 401 as an expired session, and the workflow pages request the project list when they load. Unless an administrator has enabled the project feature, this does not affect other functionality; those project-list requests are simply rejected. Make sure the Texera server is reachable only through that proxy.



Blocking and upgrading do not undo access obtained earlier. Before upgrading, review the project, project_user_access and workflow_of_project tables, which remain empty unless someone has used the feature, and remove rows you do not expect; the upgrade deletes these tables. Do not copy project grants into workflow_user_access without checking each one.

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the public project REST API of Apache Texera (incubating).



The public project API did not check that a project had been made public before granting the caller read access to it. Any authenticated user with an approved account (the REGULAR or ADMIN role; new accounts need administrator approval by default) could give themselves lasting read access to other users' private projects and to the private workflows in them, including their version and execution history. Only deployments in which users have created projects are affected; the project feature is hidden in the web UI by default.

Make sure the Texera server is reachable only through that proxy.



Blocking and upgrading do not undo access obtained earlier. An out-of-bounds heap read flaw was found in GIMP's TIM image loader. When a user opens a crafted 4bpp TIM image that causes promotion to an RGBA layer, the file-tim plug-in allocates an undersized row buffer but processes it using the larger RGBA row size. This can copy adjacent heap contents into the decoded image and may crash the plug-in.

A one-byte out-of-bounds heap read flaw was found in GIMP's uncompressed DDS image loader. When a user opens an uncompressed DDS image, the file-dds plug-in performs an unconditional one-byte look-ahead after processing the final pixel. This may cause the plug-in to crash if the byte immediately following the pixel buffer is inaccessible; no information disclosure or code execution has been demonstrated.
